1.summary: People are generally allowed to criticise the government.
1.whyCorrect: Freedom of expression protects the open communication of political opinions, subject to legal limits that protect other people.
1.background: Freedom of expression is set out in Article 5 of the Basic Law. Everyone may freely express their opinion in speech, writing and pictures – even when the government does not like it. Criticising politicians, demonstrating and publishing critical newspaper articles are therefore part of everyday life in Germany. There are still limits: insults, defamation and incitement to hatred are criminal offences. Factual or even sharp criticism, however, is protected.
1.otherOptions: Freedom of religion (Article 4) protects belief, not political statements. Paying taxes does not give anyone a special right to criticise – freedom of expression also applies to people without an income. The right to vote is a trap: it is also a democratic right, but it concerns casting a vote in elections, not speaking openly.
1.memoryTip: Look for the word “speak”: whoever may speak freely has freedom of expression.

2.summary: Parents decide on participation in religious education until the child is 14.
2.whyCorrect: The rule concerns the child’s religious upbringing, so religious education is the relevant school subject.
2.background: Religious education is a regular school subject in most state schools (Article 7 of the Basic Law). Because religion is a personal matter of conscience, nobody may be forced to take part. Until the child’s 14th birthday, the parents decide whether the child attends. From the age of 14, a child is considered “of religious age” and decides on their own religion – and therefore on religious education. Pupils who do not attend usually take a substitute subject such as ethics.
2.otherOptions: History, politics and languages are compulsory subjects. Parents cannot simply withdraw their child from them, because the state has an educational mandate. Only religious education offers this choice, because freedom of belief is involved.
2.memoryTip: 14 and religion belong together: at 14, the child decides on their own faith.

legalBasis.label: Sec. 5 Religious Education of Children Act

3.summary: In a state governed by law, public authorities are also bound by the law.
3.whyCorrect: The rule of law means that residents and the state must follow the applicable law rather than act arbitrarily.
3.background: The rule of law means that the law stands above everyone – above the residents, but also above the state itself. The government, authorities and police may only act if a law allows it (Article 20(3) of the Basic Law). Anyone who feels treated unfairly by an authority can take the matter to an independent court. This protects against arbitrary decisions, because no office and no politician is above the law.
3.otherOptions: A state that does not have to obey the law would be the opposite of the rule of law. Laws apply to everyone in Germany, not only to Germans. And courts do not make laws: that is the job of the parliaments (Bundestag, Bundesrat, state parliaments). Courts apply the laws – this is called the separation of powers.
3.memoryTip: Rule of law = the law applies to everyone, including the state.

4.summary: Freedom of expression is a fundamental right.
4.whyCorrect: It is protected by the Basic Law; possessing weapons, vigilante force and taking the law into one’s own hands are not fundamental rights.
4.background: The fundamental rights are at the beginning of the Basic Law, in Articles 1 to 19. Freedom of expression (Article 5) is one of the most important, because a democracy cannot work without free debate. Fundamental rights mainly protect people from the state: it may only restrict them within narrow limits and only by law.
4.otherOptions: Owning weapons is not a fundamental right in Germany – unlike what many people know from the USA. Anyone who wants to own a weapon needs a permit under the Weapons Act. “Fist law” and vigilante justice mean using violence to get “justice” yourself. This is forbidden, because in Germany only the state has a monopoly on the use of force: the police and courts enforce the law.
4.memoryTip: Three answers have to do with violence – the fundamental right is the only peaceful answer.

5.summary: A free election allows a choice without coercion or disadvantage.
5.whyCorrect: Voters must make their own decision and may not be forced or improperly influenced to cast a particular vote.
5.background: For federal elections, the Basic Law sets out five electoral principles: general, direct, free, equal and secret (Article 38). “Free” means that nobody may pressure, bribe or threaten voters, and nobody may suffer disadvantages because of their vote. A free election also means that you do not have to vote at all.
5.otherOptions: Accepting money for a particular vote is vote buying and a criminal offence. People who have been or are in prison are usually allowed to vote as well – only a court can take away the right to vote, and only in rare cases. Germany has no compulsory voting, unlike Belgium, for example.
5.memoryTip: The five electoral principles: general, direct, free, equal, secret. “Free” means without pressure and without obligation.

6.summary: Germany’s constitution is called the Basic Law.
6.whyCorrect: “Basic Law for the Federal Republic of Germany” is the constitution’s official name.
6.background: The German constitution is called the Basic Law (Grundgesetz, GG). It was drafted by the Parliamentary Council in Bonn and promulgated on 23 May 1949. The word “constitution” was avoided on purpose, because Germany was divided at the time and the Basic Law was meant to apply only until all of Germany adopted a constitution. Since reunification in 1990, the Basic Law has applied to the whole of Germany. 23 May is therefore “Basic Law Day”.
6.otherOptions: A federal law is an ordinary law passed by the Bundestag and Bundesrat, for example the Nationality Act. It ranks below the Basic Law and must not contradict it. A “People’s Law” or a “German Law” does not exist.
6.memoryTip: Grundgesetz = the foundation (“Grund”) of all laws. Abbreviation: GG.

7.summary: Freedom of faith and conscience is constitutionally protected.
7.whyCorrect: It is one of the fundamental rights guaranteed by the Basic Law; entertainment, work and housing are not the guarantee asked for here.
7.background: Article 4 of the Basic Law guarantees freedom of faith and conscience. Everyone may freely decide whether and what they believe, practise their religion, change it or have no religion at all. The state remains neutral: there is no state church, and nobody may be disadvantaged because of their faith. Freedom of conscience also includes the right to refuse military service with weapons.
7.otherOptions: A right to work, to housing or to entertainment is not in the Basic Law. There is freedom of occupation (Article 12): you may freely choose your profession – but the state does not have to guarantee you a job. Some state constitutions name work or housing as state objectives, but these are not enforceable fundamental rights.
7.memoryTip: Fundamental rights are mostly freedoms (“believe freely, speak freely”), not claims to things like housing or work.

8.summary: The Basic Law does not guarantee that everyone has the same amount of money.
8.whyCorrect: It protects human dignity, expression and equality before the law, but it does not prescribe equal incomes.
8.background: The three correct statements come almost word for word from the Basic Law: “Human dignity shall be inviolable” (Article 1), “All persons shall be equal before the law” (Article 3) and freedom of expression (Article 5). Germany is a social state (Article 20): it helps people in need, for example with citizen’s income (Bürgergeld) or health insurance. But the Basic Law does not promise the same income for everyone.
8.otherOptions: “Everyone should have the same amount of money” describes an idea that is not in the Basic Law. Property (Article 14) and freedom of occupation apply in Germany, and incomes may differ. In the Basic Law, equality means equal rights, not equal money.
8.memoryTip: Equal before the law – yes. Equal money – no.

9.summary: The constitutional right of asylum concerns foreign nationals facing political persecution.
9.whyCorrect: Human dignity and the freedoms of family and expression apply generally, while asylum concerns protection for persecuted foreigners.
9.background: Article 16a of the Basic Law states: “Persons persecuted on political grounds shall have the right of asylum.” Asylum protects people who are persecuted in their country of origin because of their political opinion, religion or origin. Germans do not need this protection in Germany – that is why the right of asylum only applies to foreigners. In practice, many refugees also receive protection under the Geneva Refugee Convention.
9.otherOptions: Human dignity (Article 1), protection of the family (Article 6) and freedom of expression (Article 5) are human rights: they apply to everyone in Germany, whatever their nationality. Conversely, some rights apply only to Germans, for example freedom of assembly under Article 8.
9.memoryTip: Asylum is protection from persecution in your home country – only people from other countries need it.

10.summary: A fine is compatible with the Basic Law.
10.whyCorrect: It is a sanction provided by law. Corporal punishment, torture and the death penalty violate fundamental constitutional protections.
10.background: A fine is a completely normal penalty under German criminal law: a court orders a person to pay a certain amount of money. This is compatible with the Basic Law. The death penalty, on the other hand, was explicitly abolished by the Basic Law (Article 102: “Capital punishment is abolished.”). The basis for this is human dignity in Article 1, which the state must always respect.
10.otherOptions: Torture violates human dignity and is forbidden without exception, even when serious crimes are suspected. Detained persons may not be subjected to mental or physical mistreatment (Article 104). Corporal punishment does not exist in Germany; parents are not allowed to hit their children either.
10.memoryTip: Only one answer does not physically hurt anyone: the fine.

11.summary: The constitution of the Federal Republic is called the Basic Law.
11.whyCorrect: Terms such as federal constitution or constitutional treaty are not its official name.
11.background: The constitution of the Federal Republic is called the Basic Law (Grundgesetz). It sets out the fundamental rights (Articles 1 to 19), the principles of the state such as democracy, the rule of law and federalism, and the tasks of the constitutional bodies, for example the Bundestag, the Bundesrat and the Federal President. All other laws must be compatible with the Basic Law. In case of dispute, the Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe decides. The Basic Law can only be amended with two-thirds majorities in both the Bundestag and the Bundesrat.
11.otherOptions: “Federal Constitution” (Bundesverfassung) is the name of Switzerland’s constitution, not Germany’s. A code (Gesetzbuch) is a collection of laws on one area of law, for example the Civil Code (BGB) or the Criminal Code (StGB). “Constitutional Treaty” was the name of a planned EU treaty that failed in 2005.
11.memoryTip: This question is almost the same as question 6 – the answer is always Grundgesetz (Basic Law).

12.summary: A political party cannot simply abolish freedom of the press.
12.whyCorrect: Freedom of the press is protected as a fundamental right and cannot be removed by an ordinary political majority.
12.background: Freedom of the press is set out in Article 5 of the Basic Law: newspapers, broadcasters and online media may report freely, and “there shall be no censorship”. Fundamental rights can be restricted by law within limits, but according to Article 19, “in no case may the essence of a basic right be affected”. In addition, democracy is protected by the so-called eternity clause (Article 79(3)) – and there is no democracy without a free press.
12.otherOptions: A simple majority is not even enough for a normal amendment to the Basic Law. Even with two thirds in the Bundestag (and the Bundesrat), freedom of the press could not be abolished, because its core is protected. The Bundesrat represents the federal states and cannot abolish fundamental rights either.
12.memoryTip: No majority can abolish fundamental rights – neither half nor two thirds.

13.summary: The opposition consists of members of parliament outside the governing parties.
13.whyCorrect: They scrutinise and criticise the government in parliament and offer political alternatives.
13.background: There are two sides in the Bundestag: the governing parties, which together support the federal government, and the opposition. The opposition consists of all members of parliament whose parties are not part of the government. Its job is to scrutinise and criticise the government and to make its own proposals – for example through parliamentary questions, debates or committees of inquiry. A strong opposition is important for democracy.
13.otherOptions: The governing parties are the exact opposite of the opposition. The parliamentary group with the most members usually forms the government, but it does not have to. All parties in the Bundestag have passed the 5 percent threshold – governing parties and opposition parties alike.
13.memoryTip: Opposition = the side “opposite” the government: everyone who is not governing.

14.summary: An opinion may generally also be expressed online.
14.whyCorrect: Freedom of expression applies regardless of the medium, while illegal content and violations of others’ rights remain restricted.
14.background: Freedom of expression (Article 5 of the Basic Law) means: I may freely say, write and share my opinion – on the street, in the newspaper and also online, for example on social media or in a blog. I may also criticise the government. But freedom of expression has limits: the law protects other people’s honour and bans certain symbols and hate speech.
14.otherOptions: Insulting passers-by is an insult under criminal law and can be punished. Publicly displaying symbols of unconstitutional or banned organisations – such as Nazi symbols or symbols of Hamas and the “Islamic State” – is forbidden. And an opinion that contradicts the government is explicitly allowed.
14.memoryTip: Online – yes. Insults and banned symbols – no.

15.summary: The Basic Law prohibits forced labour.
15.whyCorrect: People may not generally be compelled to work; free choice of occupation and working abroad are not the prohibition asked for.
15.background: Article 12 of the Basic Law protects freedom of occupation. It also states that nobody may be forced to do a particular kind of work, and that forced labour is only permitted for people deprived of their liberty by a court decision, for example work in prison. History is part of the background: under National Socialism, millions of people were forced to do forced labour.
15.otherOptions: Military service is not forbidden – Article 12a explicitly allows it. Free choice of occupation is not forbidden but a fundamental right. Working abroad is also allowed; anyone may leave Germany and work in another country.
15.memoryTip: What is forbidden is the force, not the work: forced labour.

16.summary: False factual claims about individuals may be restricted.
16.whyCorrect: Freedom of expression protects criticism and opinions, but not every untrue assertion that violates personality rights.
16.background: Freedom of expression is limited, among other things, by the “right to personal honour” (Article 5(2)). Anyone who publicly spreads false facts about a specific person can commit a criminal offence, for example defamation or slander. Those affected can also demand that the false claim be deleted or retracted. An opinion (“I think she is a bad politician”) is protected; an invented fact (“she stole money”) is not.
16.otherOptions: Opinions about the federal government, discussions about religions and criticism of the state are covered by freedom of expression. In fact, criticism of the government and the state is exactly what freedom of expression is meant to protect.
16.memoryTip: Opinions are free – false claims about people are not.

17.summary: The state may not arbitrarily treat citizens unequally.
17.whyCorrect: The equality principle binds state action, while petitions and the freedoms of expression and assembly are protected rights.
17.background: Article 3 of the Basic Law states: “All persons shall be equal before the law.” Nobody may be disadvantaged because of their sex, parentage, language, origin, faith, political opinions or a disability. The state must treat everyone equally – for example at public offices, at school or in court. Unequal treatment by the state is therefore forbidden.
17.otherOptions: Freedom of expression (Article 5), petitions (Article 17) and freedom of assembly (Article 8) are fundamental rights and therefore explicitly allowed. With a petition, you can address requests or complaints in writing to authorities or parliaments.
17.memoryTip: Three answers are fundamental rights – only unequal treatment is forbidden.

18.summary: Article 1 protects the inviolability of human dignity.
18.whyCorrect: Human dignity appears at the beginning of the Basic Law and binds all public authority to respect and protect it.
18.background: Article 1(1) is the most important sentence of the Basic Law: “Human dignity shall be inviolable. To respect and protect it shall be the duty of all state authority.” Every person has dignity, regardless of origin, religion or nationality. After the crimes of National Socialism, this sentence was deliberately placed at the very beginning. Under the eternity clause (Article 79(3)), Article 1 may never be changed.
18.otherOptions: The other rights are also fundamental rights, but they are in other articles: the right to life in Article 2, freedom of religion in Article 4 and freedom of expression in Article 5.
18.memoryTip: Article 1 – the first and most important: human dignity.

19.summary: Freedom of movement includes choosing where to live within Germany.
19.whyCorrect: The right concerns movement and residence, not occupation, religion or clothing.
19.background: Freedom of movement (Freizügigkeit, Article 11 of the Basic Law) means: you may decide freely where to live in Germany and move within the country. The Basic Law guarantees this right to all Germans. Citizens of the EU also enjoy EU freedom of movement. For other foreign nationals, residence law determines where they may live.
19.otherOptions: Changing your job belongs to freedom of occupation (Article 12), changing your religion to freedom of faith (Article 4). The last answer is a trap: in everyday German, “freizügig” can also mean “scantily dressed” – which has nothing to do with the fundamental right.
19.memoryTip: Freizügigkeit = moving freely: choosing and changing where you live.

20.summary: A party seeking to establish a dictatorship acts against the constitution.
20.whyCorrect: The free democratic constitutional order excludes replacing democracy with dictatorship.
20.background: A party that wants to establish a dictatorship is fighting against the free democratic basic order. According to Article 21(2) of the Basic Law, it is then unconstitutional. However, only the Federal Constitutional Court can ban a party. This happened to the Socialist Reich Party in 1952 and to the Communist Party (KPD) in 1956. Germany calls this a “defensive democracy”: democracy protects itself against its enemies.
20.otherOptions: Tolerant, committed to the rule of law and law-abiding describe the exact opposite of a party that wants a dictatorship. A dictatorship abolishes elections, fundamental rights and independent courts.

21.summary: Image 1 shows the federal coat of arms.
21.whyCorrect: The federal coat of arms is the black federal eagle on a gold background; in this image question that is number 1.
21.background: The coat of arms of the Federal Republic of Germany shows a black eagle with red claws, a red beak and a red tongue on a golden-yellow background – the federal eagle. You can see it on ID cards, coins, signs on public buildings and in the plenary hall of the Bundestag. Black, red and gold are also the colours of the federal flag.
21.otherOptions: Image 2 shows the Chi-Rho, a Christian symbol. Image 3 is the Iron Cross, the emblem of the German armed forces (Bundeswehr). Image 4 is the state coat of arms of the GDR with hammer, compass and a wreath of wheat – it has not been used since reunification in 1990.
21.memoryTip: The federal coat of arms has the same colours as the flag: black, red, gold.

22.whyCorrect: The head of state is not hereditary; Germany is not a monarchy, principality or dictatorship.
22.background: Germany is a republic. This means the head of state is not a king and does not inherit the office, but is elected for a limited period. The Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention for five years. The country’s name already says it: Federal Republic of Germany. The monarchy in Germany ended in 1918.
22.otherOptions: In a monarchy or a principality, a king or prince rules, usually by inheriting the office – for example in Liechtenstein or Monaco. Germany was a dictatorship under National Socialism (1933–1945); today the Basic Law rules this out.
22.memoryTip: Federal Republic of Germany – the answer is in the name.

23.whyCorrect: Most work for a company or public authority rather than being self-employed or working voluntarily.
23.background: Most people in work in Germany are employees: they work for a company or for a public authority and receive a wage or salary. This applies to about nine out of ten people in work. Only a small share are self-employed, for example with their own shop, practice or as freelancers.
23.otherOptions: Many companies in Germany are family businesses, but most people do not work in small family firms. Voluntary work is unpaid and is done in addition to a job. Self-employed people with their own company are a minority.
23.memoryTip: Most people are employed – by a company or by the state.

24.summary: The Federal Republic of Germany has 16 federal states.
24.whyCorrect: They include 13 territorial states and the three city states Berlin, Bremen and Hamburg.
24.background: Germany has 16 federal states: 13 territorial states such as Bavaria or North Rhine-Westphalia and 3 city states – Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen. There have been 16 since reunification in 1990, when the five eastern states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia joined and Berlin was reunited. Each state has its own constitution, parliament and government.
24.otherOptions: 14, 15 and 17 are wrong. The question catalogue also contains 10 questions for each federal state; 3 questions about your own state come up in the test.

25.summary: Alsace-Lorraine is not a German federal state.
25.whyCorrect: The region is in present-day France; North Rhine-Westphalia, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania and Saxony-Anhalt are German states.
25.background: Alsace-Lorraine (Elsass-Lothringen) is a region in France on the German border. It belonged to the German Empire from 1871 to 1918, but has been French again for over a hundred years. It has never been part of the Federal Republic of Germany. The 16 federal states are: Baden-Württemberg, Bavaria, Berlin, Brandenburg, Bremen, Hamburg, Hesse, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Lower Saxony, North Rhine-Westphalia, Rhineland-Palatinate, Saarland, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Schleswig-Holstein and Thuringia.
25.otherOptions: North Rhine-Westphalia is the most populous state, with Düsseldorf as its capital. Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania (capital Schwerin) and Saxony-Anhalt (capital Magdeburg) are among the states that joined with reunification in 1990.
25.memoryTip: Elsass = Alsace: it sounds French, and it is French.

26.summary: Germany is a democratic and social federal state.
26.whyCorrect: These constitutional principles combine democracy, the social state and a federal structure.
26.background: Article 20 of the Basic Law begins: “The Federal Republic of Germany is a democratic and social federal state.” Democratic means the people elect their representatives. Social means the state provides social security, for example through pension, health and unemployment insurance. Federal state means power is shared between the federation and the 16 states.
26.otherOptions: A communist republic or socialist state was the GDR, not the Federal Republic. Germany has not been a monarchy since 1918. The answer “social and socialist federal state” is a trap: “social” is right, “socialist” is not.
26.memoryTip: The three words from Article 20: democratic, social, federal state.

27.whyCorrect: Public responsibilities are divided between the federation and 16 states; Germany is not a monarchy, dictatorship or socialist unitary state.
27.background: Germany is a federal state: it consists of 16 states that together form the federation. The states have their own constitutions, parliaments and governments and are responsible, for example, for schools and the police. Through the Bundesrat, they take part in federal legislation. The Basic Law gives this federal order special protection: under the eternity clause it may not be abolished.
27.otherOptions: The GDR was a socialist state until 1990. Germany was a dictatorship under National Socialism. There was a monarchy with an emperor until 1918. None of these describes Germany today.
27.memoryTip: Federal Republic = a federal state of 16 states.

28.summary: Eligible voters elect the members of the Bundestag.
28.whyCorrect: In representative democracy, eligible citizens cast their votes in the federal election.
28.background: “All state authority is derived from the people,” says Article 20 of the Basic Law. That is why eligible citizens elect the members of the Bundestag, usually every four years. German citizens aged 18 and over are eligible to vote. With the first vote you choose a person in your constituency, with the second vote a party.
28.otherOptions: The military, the economy and the administration have no vote of their own in elections. Soldiers, business owners or civil servants may of course vote – but only as individual eligible citizens, not as institutions.
28.memoryTip: Democracy means rule by the people: the people vote.

29.summary: The eagle is the heraldic animal of the Federal Republic.
29.whyCorrect: The federal eagle is a traditional German state symbol and appears in the federal coat of arms.
29.background: The heraldic animal of the Federal Republic of Germany is the eagle. The federal eagle is black on a gold background and is one of the oldest German state symbols. You can see it on coins, passports and in the plenary hall of the Bundestag, where a large eagle sculpture hangs.
29.otherOptions: The lion, bear and horse are heraldic animals of individual states and cities: the bear is the symbol of Berlin, the leaping horse appears in the coats of arms of Lower Saxony and North Rhine-Westphalia, and lions appear, for example, in the coats of arms of Bavaria and Hesse.
29.memoryTip: The federation has the eagle – the states have lions, bears or horses.

30.summary: Press censorship is not a feature of democracy.
30.whyCorrect: Regular elections, free expression and multiple parties enable democratic control, while censorship prevents open public debate.
30.background: Article 5 of the Basic Law guarantees freedom of the press and states explicitly: “There shall be no censorship.” The state may therefore not tell newspapers, broadcasters and online media what to report, and may not check or ban articles before publication. Free media inform people and hold the government to account.
30.otherOptions: Regular elections, freedom of expression and multiple parties are typical features of democracy. Press censorship, by contrast, exists in dictatorships – it is not part of our democracy.
30.memoryTip: Watch for “not”: you are looking for what does not fit – censorship.

31.summary: Several parties governing together form a coalition.
31.whyCorrect: If no party has a majority in parliament on its own, parties join together in a coalition and form the government together.
31.background: In a federal election, no party usually wins more than half the seats on its own. Several parties then work together to form a majority and the government. This is called a coalition. The parties set out their joint plans in a coalition agreement. After the 2025 federal election, for example, the CDU/CSU and the SPD formed a coalition.
31.otherOptions: A parliamentary group (Fraktion) is the group of a party’s members in parliament – in a coalition it works together with other groups. A ministry is an authority headed by a minister. “Unity” is not a political term for forming a government.
31.memoryTip: Coalition = parties working together; Fraktion = a party’s members of parliament.

32.summary: The press is not a power of the state.
32.whyCorrect: The three powers of the state are legislation, executive power (government) and the judiciary; the press is independent of the state.
32.background: The Basic Law divides state power into three branches (Article 20(2)): legislation (the legislature, i.e. parliament), executive power (the executive, i.e. government and administration) and the judiciary (the courts). This separation of powers prevents any one body from gaining too much power.
32.otherOptions: The press is often called the “fourth estate” because it scrutinises those in power. But that is only a metaphor: the press is not a state power, it is independent of the state. Legislation, government and the judiciary are the three powers of the state.
32.memoryTip: Three state powers: making laws, carrying them out, judging. The press is free and not one of them.

33.summary: In Germany, the state and religious communities are separate.
33.whyCorrect: There is no state church; the state is religiously neutral and does not favour any religion.
33.background: In Germany, the state and religious communities are separate. The Basic Law adopts provisions of the Weimar Constitution for this: “There shall be no state church.” The state is religiously neutral and does not favour any religion. Still, the state and religious communities cooperate in some areas, for example on religious education in schools or the church tax, which the tax office collects for the churches.
33.otherOptions: Religious communities do not form the state, the state does not depend on them, and they do not form a single unit. That would be a theocracy or a state church, which the Basic Law rules out.
33.memoryTip: No state church: state and religion are separate.

34.whyCorrect: Germany is a republic with an elected head of state; democracy, the rule of law and the social state are core principles of the Basic Law.
34.background: Germany is not a monarchy but a republic. The head of state is not a king or queen, but the Federal President, who is elected for five years. The monarchy in Germany ended in 1918 with the end of the German Empire.
34.otherOptions: Democracy, the rule of law and the social state describe Germany correctly. These principles are in the Basic Law (Articles 20 and 28) and are among the most important features of the Federal Republic.
34.memoryTip: You are looking for what Germany is not: there has been no king since 1918.

35.summary: Social insurance is mainly financed through social security contributions.
35.whyCorrect: Employees and employers pay contributions to health, long-term care, pension and unemployment insurance; church tax, donations and membership fees are not part of it.
35.background: Social insurance is mainly financed through social security contributions, which are deducted from wages and salaries. For most types of insurance, employees and employers each pay roughly half. Social insurance includes health, long-term care, pension, unemployment and accident insurance. Accident insurance is paid by employers alone; the state also adds subsidies from taxes, for example for pensions.
35.otherOptions: Church tax goes to the churches, not to social insurance. Donations and membership fees are voluntary payments to organisations or clubs; the state does not use them to finance social insurance.
35.memoryTip: Social insurance is paid for with social contributions (Sozialabgaben) – the word is already in the name.

36.whyCorrect: It is part of social insurance and protects people when they are ill; car, building and liability insurance are private insurances for property.
36.background: Health insurance is part of social insurance and is compulsory in Germany. It pays for doctor’s visits, hospital stays and many medicines. Most people have statutory health insurance; some, such as civil servants or the self-employed, can take out private insurance. Together with pension, long-term care, unemployment and accident insurance, it provides social security.
36.otherOptions: Car, building and liability insurance are private insurances. They protect against damage to property or against compensation claims. Liability insurance is compulsory for cars, but it is still not part of social security.
36.memoryTip: Social security is about people (illness, old age, unemployment), not cars or houses.

37.summary: In most federal states, the head of government is called Minister-President.
37.whyCorrect: This applies to the 13 territorial states; in the city states of Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen the office is called mayor.
37.background: In 13 of the 16 federal states, the head of government is called Minister-President (Ministerpräsident or Ministerpräsidentin). They are elected by the state parliament and lead the state government. The three city states use other titles: in Berlin the office is called Governing Mayor, in Hamburg First Mayor and in Bremen President of the Senate.
37.otherOptions: Prime Minister is the title of the British head of government, First Minister that of Scotland or Wales. In the city states of Berlin, Hamburg and Bremen, senators are the members of the state government – something like state ministers, not the heads.

38.summary: Germany is a democratic and social federal state.
38.whyCorrect: This is stated in Article 20 of the Basic Law: the federation and 16 states together form the state.
38.background: According to Article 20 of the Basic Law, Germany is a “democratic and social federal state”. In a federal state, states join together to form one common state. The states keep their own responsibilities, for example for schools and the police; the federation is responsible, for example, for foreign policy and defence.
38.otherOptions: A confederation (Staatenbund) is a loose association of independent states without a common state. The Federal Constitutional Court calls the European Union a “Staatenverbund” (association of states). In a centralised state like France, there are no states with their own parliaments and governments.

39.summary: Every federal state has its own government.
39.whyCorrect: Foreign policy, the army and currency are matters for the federation or the EU; but each state has its own government and parliament.
39.background: Each of the 16 federal states has its own government, its own parliament (usually called Landtag) and its own constitution. The state government is responsible, for example, for schools, the police and universities. In most states it is headed by a Minister-President.
39.otherOptions: Foreign policy, defence and currency are matters for the federation or the EU. The Bundeswehr is Germany’s only army, there is a foreign minister only at federal level, and people pay with the euro throughout Germany.
39.memoryTip: Foreign policy, the army and money are federal matters – but every state has a government.

40.summary: The national anthem begins with “Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit”.
40.whyCorrect: The national anthem is the third verse of the “Song of the Germans” by Hoffmann von Fallersleben.
40.background: The German national anthem is the third verse of the “Song of the Germans” (Lied der Deutschen). The lyrics were written by August Heinrich Hoffmann von Fallersleben in 1841, and the melody is by Joseph Haydn. Since 1991, only the third verse has officially been the national anthem. It begins with the words “Einigkeit und Recht und Freiheit für das deutsche Vaterland” (Unity and justice and freedom for the German fatherland).
40.otherOptions: “Völker, hört die Signale” comes from “The Internationale”, a song of the labour movement. “Freude schöner Götterfunken” is the beginning of Beethoven’s “Ode to Joy”, the European anthem. “Deutschland einig Vaterland” is a line from the national anthem of the GDR.
40.memoryTip: Unity, justice, freedom – these words are also on the edge of the German 2-euro coin.

41.summary: Several parties represent the different opinions of citizens.
41.whyCorrect: Only with several parties do voters have a real choice between different political positions.
41.background: In a democracy, people have different opinions and interests. Parties gather these opinions, turn them into programmes and stand for election. Only if there are several parties do voters have a real choice. Article 21 of the Basic Law says that parties participate in forming the political will of the people.
41.otherOptions: Several parties do not automatically prevent bribery – there are laws and controls for that. In a democracy, demonstrations should not be prevented; they are protected by freedom of assembly. Economic competition is a matter for the economy, not the reason for having several parties.

42.summary: New laws are passed by parliament.
42.whyCorrect: At federal level, the Bundestag passes laws, often together with the Bundesrat; the government, courts and police do not pass laws.
42.background: New federal laws are passed by parliament: the Bundestag, together with the Bundesrat for many laws. Proposals for laws can come from the federal government, from the Bundestag or from the Bundesrat. The state parliaments are responsible for state laws. This is part of the separation of powers: parliament makes the laws.
42.otherOptions: The government can propose laws but does not pass them. Courts apply laws and can review whether they are compatible with the Basic Law. The police make sure laws are followed.
42.memoryTip: Parliament = makes laws; government = carries them out; courts = judge.

43.summary: A party can be banned if it fights against the constitution.
43.whyCorrect: Only the Federal Constitutional Court can ban a party that seeks to abolish the free democratic basic order.
43.background: A party can be banned if it seeks to abolish the free democratic basic order or endangers the existence of Germany (Article 21 of the Basic Law). Only the Federal Constitutional Court can impose a ban. An application can be made by the Bundestag, the Bundesrat or the federal government. The hurdles are high so that parties cannot simply be banned for political reasons.
43.otherOptions: An expensive election campaign, criticism of the head of state or a programme with new ideas are allowed in a democracy. Criticism and new political directions are part of the democratic competition between parties.
43.memoryTip: Only those who fight the constitution are banned – not those who criticise.

44.summary: The Federal President is not elected directly.
44.whyCorrect: The head of state is elected by the Federal Convention; citizens directly elect members of the European Parliament, state parliaments and the Bundestag.
44.background: The Federal President is not elected directly by the people but by the Federal Convention. It is made up of all members of the Bundestag and the same number of delegates chosen by the state parliaments. The term of office is five years; one re-election is possible.
44.otherOptions: Citizens directly elect the members of the European Parliament, the state parliament and the Bundestag. EU citizens living in Germany may also vote in local elections and European elections.
44.memoryTip: President → Federal Convention; parliaments → the people.

45.summary: Long-term care insurance is part of social insurance.
45.whyCorrect: Together with health, pension, unemployment and accident insurance, it is one of the five branches of social insurance.
45.background: Long-term care insurance is part of social insurance. It was introduced in 1995 as the newest branch and helps people who need long-term care because of illness, disability or old age – at home or in a care home. Anyone with statutory health insurance is automatically covered by long-term care insurance. Employees and employers share the contributions; people without children pay a small surcharge.
45.otherOptions: Accident insurance is itself a branch of social insurance, but long-term care insurance is not part of it. Household contents, liability and fire insurance are private insurances against damage to property.
45.memoryTip: Five branches of social insurance: health, long-term care, pension, unemployment and accident insurance.

46.summary: The state builds, for example, roads and schools.
46.whyCorrect: Public infrastructure is a task of the state; food, clothing and vehicles are produced by private companies.
46.background: The state provides public infrastructure: it builds and maintains roads, bridges, schools and hospitals. Depending on the task, the federation, the states or the municipalities are responsible – motorways, for example, are federal, while school buildings are usually provided by towns and municipalities. This is paid for mainly from taxes.
46.otherOptions: In the social market economy, food, clothing, cars and buses are produced and sold by private companies. The state does not hand out free newspapers to everyone; the press is independent of the state.
46.memoryTip: The state builds what everyone needs: roads and schools.

47.summary: The state does not pay for holidays.
47.whyCorrect: Child benefit, funding for museums and support for athletes are tasks of the state; private holidays are not.
47.background: The state supports families, culture and sport. For example, it pays child benefit (Kindergeld), funds museums and theatres and supports athletes. But people have to pay for their own holidays – that is not a task of the state.
47.otherOptions: Child benefit is paid to parents by the Family Benefits Office (Familienkasse). Museums are funded mainly by the states and cities. Sport is funded at both elite and grassroots level, for example through clubs. All three are tasks of the state.
47.memoryTip: You are looking for what does not fit: you pay for your holidays yourself.

48.summary: The citizens’ assembly is not a constitutional body.
48.whyCorrect: Constitutional bodies include the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, the Federal President, the federal government and the Federal Constitutional Court.
48.background: Constitutional bodies are the highest bodies of the federation set out in the Basic Law: the Bundestag, the Bundesrat, the federal government, the Federal President, the Federal Convention and the Federal Constitutional Court. They share the tasks of the state and keep a check on each other. The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe ensures that all other bodies respect the Basic Law.
48.otherOptions: The Bundesrat, the Federal President and the federal government are constitutional bodies. A “citizens’ assembly” (Bürgerversammlung) exists only at local level in some states, as a meeting of a municipality’s residents. It is not a constitutional body of the federation.
48.memoryTip: Constitutional bodies start with “Bundes-” (federal) – the citizens’ assembly does not fit.

49.summary: The federal states decide school policy.
49.whyCorrect: Education is a matter for the states in Germany; that is why they have their own school laws and curricula.
49.background: In Germany, the federal states are responsible for schools. This is called the cultural sovereignty of the states. That is why each state has its own school laws, curricula, types of schools and holiday dates. To keep qualifications comparable, the states coordinate in the Standing Conference of Ministers of Education (Kultusministerkonferenz).
49.otherOptions: Teachers teach according to the states’ rules but do not make school policy. The Federal Ministry for Family Affairs is responsible for families, senior citizens, women and youth, not schools. Universities train teachers but do not decide school policy.
49.memoryTip: Schools are a matter for the states – that is why summer holidays differ everywhere.

50.summary: Germany’s economic system is called the social market economy.
50.whyCorrect: It combines a free market with social balance provided by the state; the GDR had a planned economy.
50.background: Germany’s economic system is called the social market economy. Companies produce and sell freely, and prices are set by supply and demand. But the state ensures social balance, for example through social insurance, protection against dismissal, the minimum wage and rules for fair competition. Ludwig Erhard, the first economics minister of the Federal Republic, is considered the father of the social market economy.
50.otherOptions: In a planned economy or a centrally directed economy, the state decides what is produced and what it costs – as in the GDR. A “free central economy” does not exist; free and centrally directed do not go together.
50.memoryTip: Market + social balance = social market economy.

51.summary: Arbitrary arrests by a private police force are not part of a state governed by the rule of law.
51.whyCorrect: Only state authorities may arrest people, on a legal basis; a court must decide on any deprivation of liberty.
51.background: In a democratic state governed by the rule of law, only the state has the right to use force and arrest people – and only when a law allows it. Article 104 of the Basic Law sets out exactly how this must happen: a judge decides on any longer deprivation of liberty, and anyone arrested must be brought before a court by the end of the following day at the latest. Private security services may not “arrest” anyone.
51.otherOptions: Criticising the government and demonstrating peacefully are fundamental rights (freedom of expression and assembly). Arresting someone who has committed a crime is also in line with the rule of law – what matters is that there is a reason and the procedure follows the law.
51.memoryTip: Look for “without reason” and “private police”: neither fits the rule of law.

52.summary: Popular sovereignty means: all state authority is derived from the people.
52.whyCorrect: This is stated in Article 20 of the Basic Law; the people are the source of all state power.
52.background: Popular sovereignty means that the people are the “sovereign”, i.e. they hold the highest power in the state. Article 20(2) of the Basic Law says: “All state authority is derived from the people. It shall be exercised by the people through elections and other votes and through specific legislative, executive and judicial bodies.” So the people do not govern directly every day, but elect representatives who act on their behalf.
52.otherOptions: The Bundestag exercises state authority, but it received this authority from the people – through elections. The Federal Constitutional Court checks that the Basic Law is respected, but it is not the source of state authority. There has been no Prussian king since 1918, and Prussia was dissolved in 1947.
52.memoryTip: Sovereign = the boss. In a democracy, the boss is the people.

53.summary: The rule of law means: the state must obey the laws.
53.whyCorrect: The government, authorities and police are also bound by law and justice and can be reviewed by the courts.
53.background: Under the rule of law, the law stands above everyone – including the state. Article 20(3) of the Basic Law binds the legislature to the constitution and the government, administration and courts to law and justice. If an authority acts against the law, those affected can go to independent courts. This is how the rule of law protects citizens from arbitrary action.
53.otherOptions: “The state is right” is exactly the wrong way round: the state is not automatically right, it has to follow the law. The German word “Recht” (law) in “Rechtsstaat” has nothing to do with right-wing parties. Citizens deciding on laws directly describes direct democracy – at federal level, however, parliament passes the laws.
53.memoryTip: Rechtsstaat does not mean “the state is right”, but “the state follows the law”.

54.summary: “Directive” is not a power of the state.
54.whyCorrect: The three powers of the state are the legislature, the executive and the judiciary.
54.background: The Basic Law divides state power into three branches (separation of powers): the legislature makes the laws – the Bundestag and Bundesrat as well as the state parliaments. The executive carries out the laws – the government, ministries, authorities and police. The judiciary administers justice – the courts. The branches check each other so that nobody gains too much power.
54.otherOptions: Legislature, judiciary and executive are the three real powers. “Directive” sounds similar but is an invented answer. You may know the word from EU law, where certain legal acts are called directives – but that is not a power of the state.
54.memoryTip: Legislature = makes laws, executive = carries them out, judiciary = judges.

55.summary: The picture shows the seat of the Bundestag in Berlin, the Reichstag building.
55.whyCorrect: You can recognise it by its glass dome and the inscription “Dem deutschen Volke” (To the German people).
55.background: The Bundestag meets in the Reichstag building in Berlin. The building was completed in 1894, burned in 1933 and was badly damaged in the Second World War. After reunification it was rebuilt and given the walk-in glass dome designed by the architect Norman Foster. The Bundestag has worked here since 1999. Above the entrance it says “Dem deutschen Volke” – a reminder that parliament serves the people.
55.otherOptions: The Federal Constitutional Court is in Karlsruhe, in a low, modern building. The Bundesrat meets in the former Prussian House of Lords in Berlin, and the Federal Chancellery is a modern concrete and glass building opposite the Reichstag.

56.summary: The public order office (Ordnungsamt) is part of the municipal administration.
56.whyCorrect: It is responsible for public safety and order in the town or municipality.
56.background: The Ordnungsamt is an authority of the town or municipality. It deals with public order locally: for example, it checks parking, follows up noise complaints, handles business registrations or markets and enforces rules such as dog regulations. Many cities have a municipal enforcement service for this. The Ordnungsamt works closely with the police.
56.otherOptions: A parish office (Pfarramt) belongs to a church congregation, not to the state. The tax office (Finanzamt) is an authority of the federal state and collects taxes. The Federal Foreign Office (Auswärtiges Amt) is the federal foreign ministry in Berlin.

57.summary: Usually a member of the largest parliamentary group becomes President of the Bundestag.
57.whyCorrect: This is a parliamentary tradition: the largest group nominates the President.
57.background: The President of the Bundestag chairs the sessions of parliament, represents the Bundestag and exercises authority over the building. The President is elected by the members at the start of each legislative term. By long tradition, the largest parliamentary group nominates someone from its own ranks. Julia Klöckner (CDU) has been President of the Bundestag since 2025.
57.otherOptions: The first session is opened by the “Father of the House” (Alterspräsident) – today the member with the longest service in the Bundestag. But they only chair the session until the President is elected. State Minister-Presidents are not members of the Bundestag, and former chancellors traditionally do not become President of the Bundestag.
57.memoryTip: Largest group → usually provides both the Chancellor and the President of the Bundestag.

58.summary: Federal ministers are appointed by the Federal President.
58.whyCorrect: The President acts on the proposal of the Federal Chancellor (Article 64 of the Basic Law).
58.background: The federal government consists of the Federal Chancellor and the federal ministers. The Chancellor decides who becomes a minister, usually in agreement with the coalition partners. The ministers are then formally appointed by the Federal President, who hands them their certificate of appointment. They then take their oath of office in the Bundestag.
58.otherOptions: The President of the Federal Constitutional Court heads the court and has nothing to do with forming the government. The President of the Bundesrat chairs the Bundesrat, the President of the Bundestag chairs the sessions of the Bundestag – neither appoints ministers.
58.memoryTip: The Chancellor proposes – the President appoints.

59.summary: The first Jewish community on the territory of today’s Germany is about 1,700 years old.
59.whyCorrect: A decree by the Roman emperor Constantine from the year 321 mentions Jews in Cologne.
59.background: In 321, the Roman emperor Constantine issued a law allowing Jews in Cologne to be appointed to the city council. This is the oldest written evidence of Jewish life north of the Alps. That is why in 2021 the festival year “1700 Years of Jewish Life in Germany” was celebrated throughout the country. Jewish life has thus been part of the history of this country for almost two millennia – despite persecution in the Middle Ages and the genocide under National Socialism.
59.otherOptions: 300, 700 and 1,150 years are too short. In the Middle Ages, for example, there were already important Jewish communities in Speyer, Worms and Mainz – but the first traces are much older and date back to Roman times.
59.memoryTip: 321 AD, Cologne, Emperor Constantine → about 1,700 years.

60.summary: The Bundestag and the Bundesrat belong to the legislature.
60.whyCorrect: They are the federal law-making bodies.
60.background: Legislature means the law-making power. At federal level, the Bundestag passes the laws. The Bundesrat, in which the governments of the 16 states are represented, takes part in this: some laws require its consent, for others it can raise an objection. This way the states have a say in federal legislation.
60.otherOptions: The executive carries out laws (government and administration), the judiciary administers justice (courts). “Directive” is not one of the three powers.
60.memoryTip: Bundestag and Bundesrat make laws → legislature (Latin “lex” = law).

61.summary: Popular sovereignty means: state authority is derived from the people.
61.whyCorrect: The people are the source of state power and exercise it mainly through elections (Article 20 of the Basic Law).
61.background: This question asks the same as question 52, just with different answers. Popular sovereignty means: the sovereign is not a king, not a party and not a court, but the people. In elections, they decide who sits in parliament and thus who governs. In some federal states and municipalities, the people can also vote directly in referendums.
61.otherOptions: A king ruling over the people is the opposite of popular sovereignty. The Federal Constitutional Court does not stand above the constitution, it is bound by it. Interest groups such as trade unions or employers’ associations may represent their interests, but they have no state authority.

62.summary: The election of a federal state’s parliament is called a state election (Landtagswahl).
62.whyCorrect: In most states the state parliament is called the Landtag.
62.background: Each federal state has its own parliament. In 13 states it is called Landtag, in Berlin Abgeordnetenhaus and in Hamburg and Bremen Bürgerschaft. State elections usually take place every five years, in Bremen every four years. The elected Landtag passes state laws, for example on schools and the police, and elects the Minister-President.
62.otherOptions: In a local election (Kommunalwahl) you elect the council of a town, municipality or district. In the European election you elect the European Parliament, in the federal election the Bundestag.

63.summary: The courts are not part of the executive but of the judiciary.
63.whyCorrect: The police, tax office and ministries carry out laws and are therefore part of the executive.
63.background: Executive means the power that carries out the laws. It includes the federal and state governments with their ministries and all authorities that apply laws in everyday life – for example the police, the tax office, the job centre or the citizens’ office. The courts, on the other hand, form a separate power, the judiciary. Judges are independent and subject only to the law (Article 97 of the Basic Law).
63.otherOptions: The police, the tax office and ministries are typical examples of the executive: they apply laws. Courts, by contrast, decide disputes and can also review decisions made by the executive.
63.memoryTip: The executive carries out, the judiciary judges – courts judge.

64.summary: Today Germany is divided into the federation, the states and the municipalities.
64.whyCorrect: These are the three levels of the state: the country as a whole, the 16 federal states and the towns, municipalities and districts.
64.background: Germany has a three-level structure. The federation is responsible for matters that concern the whole country, such as foreign policy, defence and currency. The 16 states deal with, for example, schools, the police and universities. The municipalities – towns, municipalities and districts – handle local matters such as nurseries, waste collection or citizens’ offices. The Basic Law guarantees municipalities the right to self-government (Article 28).
64.otherOptions: There were four occupation zones after the Second World War, from 1945 to 1949. There was an eastern and a western state (GDR and Federal Republic) from 1949 to 1990. Cantons exist in Switzerland, not in Germany.

65.summary: Forming the federal cabinet is not a task of the Bundestag.
65.whyCorrect: The Chancellor selects the ministers; they are appointed by the Federal President.
65.background: The Bundestag has three main tasks: it passes laws and can introduce bills itself, it scrutinises the federal government, and it elects the Federal Chancellor (Article 63). The cabinet – the federal government made up of the Chancellor and ministers – is put together by the Chancellor. The Federal President appoints the ministers on the Chancellor’s proposal.
65.otherOptions: Drafting laws, scrutinising the government and electing the Chancellor are tasks of the Bundestag. Scrutiny happens, for example, through question time, parliamentary questions and committees of inquiry.
65.memoryTip: The Bundestag elects the Chancellor – the Chancellor forms the cabinet.

66.summary: The largest Jewish communities in Germany are in Berlin and Munich.
66.whyCorrect: Each of these cities has several thousand members of Jewish communities.
66.background: Today around 90,000 people in Germany are members of a Jewish community; many came from the former Soviet Union after 1990. The largest communities are the Jewish Community of Berlin and the Israelite Religious Community of Munich and Upper Bavaria. Munich has had the large Ohel Jakob Synagogue in the city centre since 2006, and Berlin has the New Synagogue with its golden dome.
66.otherOptions: Hamburg, Essen, Nuremberg and Stuttgart also have Jewish communities, but smaller ones. Worms and Speyer are a trap: together with Mainz they were the most important Jewish centres in the Middle Ages (the “ShUM cities”, now a UNESCO World Heritage Site), but today they have only small communities.
66.memoryTip: Germany’s largest cities, Berlin and Munich, also have the largest communities.

67.summary: School policy is mainly a task of the federal states.
67.whyCorrect: Education is part of the states’ cultural sovereignty; defence and foreign policy are federal matters.
67.background: Under the Basic Law, the states are responsible for everything that is not expressly assigned to the federation (Articles 30 and 70). This includes in particular schools, universities, the police and culture. That is why each state has its own school laws, curricula and holiday dates. The states coordinate in the Standing Conference of Ministers of Education so that qualifications are recognised throughout Germany.
67.otherOptions: Defence and foreign policy are exclusively federal tasks (Article 73) – there is only one Bundeswehr and one Federal Foreign Office. Economic policy is mainly made by the federation and the EU; the states have only smaller responsibilities there.
67.memoryTip: Schools = a matter for the states.

68.summary: The state supervises the school system because the Basic Law makes this its task.
68.whyCorrect: Article 7 states: “The entire school system shall be under the supervision of the state.”
68.background: According to Article 7(1) of the Basic Law, the entire school system is under the supervision of the state – in practice, the federal states. The state decides what is taught, trains teachers and ensures that qualifications are comparable. This supervision also applies to private schools: they are allowed (Article 7(4)), but need state approval and must offer equivalent education. Germany also has compulsory schooling.
68.otherOptions: Germany does not have only state schools; there are also private schools, such as church schools or Waldorf schools. Not all pupils must obtain a qualification – there is compulsory schooling, but no obligation to graduate. The fact that states have different schools is a result of state responsibility, not the reason for supervision.
68.memoryTip: Why? Because it is in the Basic Law – Article 7.

69.summary: The lowest political level in Germany is the municipalities.
69.whyCorrect: The administrative structure has three levels: the federation, the states and the municipalities.
69.background: Municipalities (Gemeinden) are the smallest political units with their own self-government (Article 28 of the Basic Law). They handle local matters: nurseries, local roads, cemeteries, citizens’ offices or waste collection. In local elections, residents elect the municipal or city council and in most states also elect the mayor directly.
69.otherOptions: City councils (Stadträte) are the elected bodies of a city – an organ of the municipality, not the level itself. District administrators (Landräte) head a rural district, and district offices (Bezirksämter) are the administrations of the districts in Berlin and Hamburg. None of these is the name of the lowest level.
69.memoryTip: Federation – state – municipality: the municipality is at the bottom and closest to the people.

70.summary: The Federal President proposes the Chancellor to the Bundestag for election.
70.whyCorrect: This is set out in Article 63 of the Basic Law; the Bundestag then holds the vote.
70.background: The photo shows Federal President Gustav Heinemann handing Helmut Schmidt his certificate of appointment as Federal Chancellor in 1974. After a federal election, the Federal President – usually after talks with the parties – proposes a person to the Bundestag for election as Chancellor. Once elected, the President appoints them. Other tasks of the Federal President: signing laws, appointing and dismissing ministers, representing Germany under international law and receiving state guests.
70.otherOptions: The Federal Chancellor and the ministers run the government, not the Federal President. Scrutinising the governing party is mainly the job of parliament and the opposition. The Chancellor selects the ministers; the President only formally appoints them.
70.memoryTip: The President proposes and appoints – the Chancellor governs.

71.summary: The Federal Chancellor spends most of their time in Berlin.
71.whyCorrect: That is where the Federal Chancellery and the Bundestag are located.
71.background: Since parliament and government moved from Bonn, the Federal Chancellor has worked in Berlin. The Federal Chancellery is in the government district directly opposite the Reichstag building, where the Bundestag meets. Cabinet meetings take place there and the Chancellor has their office there. The Bundestag moved to Berlin in 1999, and the Chancellery moved into its new building in 2001.
71.otherOptions: Bonn was the capital until 1990 and the seat of parliament and government until 1999. Today Bonn is a “Federal City” and still has some ministries, but neither the Chancellery nor the Bundestag. Meseberg Palace is the federal government’s guest house, and Bellevue Palace is the official residence of the Federal President – the Chancellor is only there for special occasions.
71.memoryTip: Capital Berlin: Bundestag, Chancellery, Federal President – all there.

72.summary: The current Federal Chancellor is Friedrich Merz.
72.whyCorrect: Friedrich Merz (CDU) was elected Federal Chancellor by the Bundestag in May 2025.
72.background: Friedrich Merz has been Federal Chancellor since 6 May 2025. He leads a coalition of the CDU/CSU and the SPD, formed after the federal election in February 2025. The Federal Chancellor determines the general guidelines of policy and is responsible for them (Article 65 of the Basic Law). The Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag, not directly by the people.
72.otherOptions: Gerhard Schröder (SPD) was Federal Chancellor from 1998 to 2005, Angela Merkel (CDU) from 2005 to 2021 – the first woman in this office. Olaf Scholz (SPD) governed between Merkel and Merz. Ursula von der Leyen was a federal minister and has been President of the European Commission since 2019.
72.memoryTip: As of 2025: Chancellor Merz. If this changes, the official question catalogue applies in the test.

73.summary: The two largest parliamentary groups in the Bundestag are currently the CDU/CSU and the AfD.
73.whyCorrect: After the 2025 federal election, the CDU/CSU has the most members and the AfD the second most.
73.background: A parliamentary group (Fraktion) is the association of a party’s members in the Bundestag (or of two allied parties such as the CDU and CSU). In the federal election in February 2025, the Union of CDU and CSU became the strongest force and the AfD the second strongest. They are followed by the SPD, Alliance 90/The Greens and The Left. The CDU/CSU and SPD govern, which makes the AfD the largest opposition group.
73.otherOptions: The Left and the Greens are the smallest groups in the current Bundestag. The SPD is the third-largest force and the Union’s coalition partner. The combination “The Left and CDU/CSU” is also wrong.
73.memoryTip: As of the 2025 federal election: 1st CDU/CSU, 2nd AfD. This may change after the next election.

74.summary: The parliament for the whole of Germany is called the Bundestag.
74.whyCorrect: The German Bundestag is the elected representative body at federal level.
74.background: The Bundestag is usually elected every four years by eligible German citizens and has had 630 members since the 2025 election. It passes federal laws, elects the Federal Chancellor, adopts the federal budget and scrutinises the government. It meets in the Reichstag building in Berlin.
74.otherOptions: The Federal Convention only meets to elect the Federal President. The Volkskammer (People’s Chamber) was the parliament of the GDR. The Federal Court of Justice in Karlsruhe is not a parliament but Germany’s highest court for civil and criminal cases.

75.summary: Germany’s current head of state is Frank-Walter Steinmeier.
75.whyCorrect: Frank-Walter Steinmeier has been Federal President since 2017 and was re-elected in 2022.
75.background: In Germany, the head of state is the Federal President. Frank-Walter Steinmeier (SPD) was elected by the Federal Convention in 2017 and confirmed for a second term in 2022. He previously served, among other things, as foreign minister. The Federal President’s role is mainly representative: he represents Germany abroad, signs laws and appoints the Chancellor and the ministers. A term lasts five years; only one re-election is possible.
75.otherOptions: Joachim Gauck was Federal President from 2012 to 2017, i.e. Steinmeier’s predecessor. Bärbel Bas was President of the Bundestag from 2021 to 2025 and has been Federal Minister of Labour and Social Affairs since 2025. Bodo Ramelow was Minister-President of Thuringia.
75.memoryTip: As of 2025: Federal President Steinmeier. The official question catalogue applies in the test.

76.summary: CDU stands for Christian Democratic Union (Christlich Demokratische Union).
76.whyCorrect: The CDU is one of Germany’s major parties and was founded in 1945.
76.background: The Christian Democratic Union (CDU) was founded after the Second World War. It aimed to bring Catholic and Protestant Christians together in a party of the centre. The CDU has provided many federal chancellors: Konrad Adenauer, Ludwig Erhard, Kurt Georg Kiesinger, Helmut Kohl, Angela Merkel and, since 2025, Friedrich Merz. The CDU does not run in Bavaria – its sister party, the CSU, runs there. In the Bundestag, the CDU and CSU form a joint parliamentary group, known as the “Union”.
76.otherOptions: “Christian German Union” sounds similar, but the D stands for “Democratic”, not “German”. A “Club of German Entrepreneurs” and a “Christian German Environmental Protection” are invented answers.

77.summary: The Bundeswehr is the German army (armed forces).
77.whyCorrect: It was founded in 1955 and serves mainly to defend Germany and its allies.
77.background: The Bundeswehr is the armed forces of the Federal Republic of Germany. According to Article 87a of the Basic Law, the federation establishes armed forces for defence. The Bundeswehr is considered a “parliamentary army”: armed deployments abroad must first be approved by the Bundestag. In peacetime the Minister of Defence holds command; in a state of defence, the Federal Chancellor. With the Bundeswehr, Germany is a member of NATO.
77.otherOptions: The police are responsible for internal security and mostly belong to the federal states; there is also the Federal Police. A port is a place for ships, and a citizens’ initiative is a group of citizens working on a particular issue.
77.memoryTip: Bundes-Wehr = the federation’s defence (Wehr) = the army.

78.summary: SPD stands for Social Democratic Party of Germany (Sozialdemokratische Partei Deutschlands).
78.whyCorrect: The SPD is Germany’s oldest party; its roots go back to 1863.
78.background: The Social Democratic Party of Germany (SPD) grew out of the labour movement of the 19th century. It traditionally campaigns for workers’ rights and social justice. The SPD provided the federal chancellors Willy Brandt, Helmut Schmidt, Gerhard Schröder and Olaf Scholz. Since 2025 it has governed together with the CDU/CSU at federal level.
78.otherOptions: “Socialist Party” is wrong – the SPD is social democratic, not socialist. The GDR had the SED (Socialist Unity Party of Germany). “Social Policy Party” and “Socially Fair Party” are invented names.
78.memoryTip: S-P-D: Social Democratic Party of Germany.

79.summary: FDP stands for Free Democratic Party (Freie Demokratische Partei).
79.whyCorrect: The FDP is a liberal party and was founded in 1948.
79.background: The Free Democratic Party (FDP) holds liberal positions: it emphasises individual freedom, civil rights and a market-oriented economic policy. The first Federal President, Theodor Heuss, came from the FDP. The party was often the junior coalition partner in federal governments, most recently from 2021 to 2024. In the 2025 federal election it failed to pass the 5 percent threshold and has not been represented in the Bundestag since.
79.otherOptions: “Free Germany Party”, “Peaceful Demonstrative Party” and “Leading Democratic Party” are invented names. Remember: the D stands for “Democratic”, the P for “Party”.

80.summary: The Federal Constitutional Court is responsible for interpreting the Basic Law.
80.whyCorrect: The court in Karlsruhe reviews whether laws and state action are compatible with the Basic Law.
80.background: The Federal Constitutional Court in Karlsruhe was established in 1951 and is often called the “guardian of the constitution”. It can declare laws unconstitutional, decides disputes between constitutional bodies and can ban parties. Anyone can lodge a constitutional complaint if they feel their fundamental rights have been violated by the state (Article 93). Its 16 judges are elected half by the Bundestag and half by the Bundesrat, each with a two-thirds majority.
80.otherOptions: Local courts (Amtsgerichte) and higher regional courts (Oberlandesgerichte) are ordinary courts for civil and criminal cases, such as tenancy disputes or theft. Administrative courts decide disputes between citizens and authorities. In the end, only the Federal Constitutional Court decides on the Basic Law.
80.memoryTip: Constitution = Basic Law → Federal Constitutional Court.

81.summary: The Federal Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag.
81.whyCorrect: The Federal President proposes a person, and the Bundestag elects them by a majority of its members (Article 63).
81.background: In Germany, the Chancellor is not elected directly by the people but by the Bundestag. The person elected is the one who receives the votes of a majority of all members – the so-called chancellor majority. That is why it is so important that the governing parties have a majority in the Bundestag. Indirectly, however, voters help decide who becomes Chancellor through their vote in the federal election.
81.otherOptions: The Bundesrat represents the states and does not elect the Chancellor. The Federal Convention elects the Federal President, not the Chancellor. The people elect the Bundestag, but not the Chancellor directly.

82.summary: The federal cabinet is led by the Federal Chancellor.
82.whyCorrect: The Chancellor determines the general guidelines of policy and conducts the business of the federal government (Article 65).
82.background: The federal cabinet is the federal government: the Federal Chancellor and the federal ministers. It usually meets once a week in the Chancellery. The Chancellor has the so-called authority to set policy guidelines – setting the broad political direction. Within this direction, each minister runs their own ministry independently.
82.otherOptions: The President of the Bundestag chairs the sessions of the Bundestag, and the President of the Bundesrat those of the Bundesrat. The Federal President is the head of state but is not part of the government and does not lead the cabinet.
82.memoryTip: Chancellor = head of the government and the cabinet.

83.summary: The German Federal Chancellor is elected by the Bundestag.
83.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 81: the vote takes place in the Bundestag, on the proposal of the Federal President (Article 63).
83.background: After a federal election, the parties negotiate a coalition. Once they have agreed, the Federal President proposes a person to the Bundestag – usually the lead candidate of the strongest party. If that person receives a majority of the votes of all members, the Federal President appoints them Chancellor. The Bundestag can also remove the Chancellor – but only by electing a successor at the same time (constructive vote of no confidence, Article 67).
83.otherOptions: The people only elect the Bundestag. The Federal Convention elects the Federal President. The federal government is only formed by the Chancellor – so it cannot elect the Chancellor.
83.memoryTip: The Bundestag elects the Chancellor – and can only remove them by electing a successor.

84.summary: The Federal President’s main task is to represent the country.
84.whyCorrect: The President represents Germany at home and abroad; the country is governed by the federal government.
84.background: The Federal President is the head of state. The President represents Germany under international law, receives state guests, visits other countries and gives important speeches, for example on days of remembrance. The President signs laws and checks that they have been passed properly, and appoints the Chancellor, ministers, federal judges and civil servants. But the President has little political power in everyday politics – the Basic Law deliberately arranged it this way after the experience of the Weimar Republic.
84.otherOptions: The country is governed by the federal government headed by the Chancellor. Laws are usually drafted by ministries or members of parliament and passed by parliament. Compliance with laws is monitored by authorities, the police and above all the courts.

85.summary: The Bundesrat is made up of government representatives of the federal states.
85.whyCorrect: Members of the 16 state governments sit in the Bundesrat (Article 51).
85.background: Through the Bundesrat, the states take part in federal legislation. It is not made up of elected members of parliament, but of members of the state governments – for example Minister-Presidents and state ministers. Each state has three to six votes depending on its population, 69 in total. A state must cast its votes as a block. The Bundesrat meets in Berlin in the former Prussian House of Lords.
85.otherOptions: The members of the Bundestag form the Bundestag, not the Bundesrat. Federal ministers belong to the federal government. Party members as such have no seat in the Bundesrat.
85.memoryTip: Bundesrat = council of the states: the state governments sit there.

86.summary: The Federal President is elected by the Federal Convention.
86.whyCorrect: The Federal Convention meets only for this purpose, usually every five years (Article 54).
86.background: The Federal Convention consists of all members of the Bundestag and the same number of members chosen by the state parliaments. The states often also send well-known figures from culture, sport or society. A candidate is elected with an absolute majority in the first or second round; in the third round a simple majority is enough. The Federal Convention meets in the Reichstag building in Berlin.
86.otherOptions: The Bundesrat represents the states in legislation but does not elect the President. “Federal parliament” means the Bundestag – its members are part of the Federal Convention, but they do not elect the President on their own. The Federal Constitutional Court is a court and does not elect anyone.
86.memoryTip: President ← Federal Convention (Bundestag + representatives of the states).

87.summary: The head of state of the Federal Republic is the Federal President.
87.whyCorrect: The President ranks first in protocol and represents the state externally.
87.background: In the order of precedence of offices, the Federal President comes first, followed by the President of the Bundestag, the Federal Chancellor, the President of the Bundesrat and the President of the Federal Constitutional Court. The Federal President’s official residence is Bellevue Palace in Berlin.
