179.whyCorrect: The surrender of the German armed forces took effect on 8 May 1945.
179.background: The German armed forces signed the unconditional surrender on 7 May 1945 in Reims and again on the night of 8–9 May in Berlin-Karlshorst. “Unconditional” meant that Germany could set no conditions, and the victorious powers took over supreme governmental authority. This ended the fighting in Europe. Today the Berlin-Karlshorst Museum, among others, commemorates this moment.
179.otherOptions: Hitler had already taken his own life on 30 April 1945, but the war continued for more than a week afterwards. There was no orderly withdrawal from the occupied territories. A revolution ended the First World War in 1918 (the November Revolution), not the Second.

180.summary: The first Federal Chancellor of the Federal Republic was Konrad Adenauer.
180.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 165: Adenauer (CDU) governed from 1949 to 1963.
180.background: Konrad Adenauer shaped the early years of the Federal Republic so strongly that people speak of the “Adenauer era”. In 1955 he travelled to Moscow and secured the release of the last roughly 10,000 German prisoners of war. In 1963 he concluded the Élysée Treaty with French President Charles de Gaulle, the foundation of Franco-German friendship.
180.otherOptions: Ludwig Erhard was Adenauer’s economics minister and succeeded him in 1963 as the second Federal Chancellor. Willy Brandt (1969–1974) and Gerhard Schröder (1998–2005) were later SPD chancellors.

181.summary: With his genuflection, Willy Brandt asked Poland and the Polish Jews for forgiveness.
181.whyCorrect: Kneeling before the memorial to the heroes of the Warsaw Ghetto was a gesture of humility and a plea for reconciliation.
181.background: On 7 December 1970, Federal Chancellor Willy Brandt was in Warsaw to sign the Treaty of Warsaw, in which the Federal Republic recognised the border with Poland. At the memorial to the 1943 Warsaw Ghetto Uprising he laid a wreath – and then unexpectedly knelt down. Without words, he expressed shame for the German crimes. The photo went around the world. In 1971 Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize for his policy of reconciliation with the East.
181.otherOptions: Brandt did not submit to the Allies and did not show humility towards the Warsaw Pact, the Eastern military alliance. He did also visit the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier, but the famous genuflection took place at the Ghetto memorial.

182.summary: The Jewish house of prayer is called a synagogue.
182.whyCorrect: The Jewish community gathers in the synagogue to pray, read the Torah and learn.
182.background: The word synagogue comes from Greek and means “assembly”. The most important service takes place on the Sabbath, which begins on Friday evening. At its centre is the Torah, which is kept on scrolls in the Torah ark. The community is often led by a rabbi. Many synagogues in Germany are under police protection today because antisemitic attacks keep happening.
182.otherOptions: A church is the Christian house of worship; a basilica is a particular architectural style or an honorary title for certain churches. A mosque is the house of prayer of Muslims.
182.memoryTip: Church – Christians, mosque – Muslims, synagogue – Jews.

183.summary: The “economic miracle” in the Federal Republic took place in the 1950s.
183.whyCorrect: After the currency reform of 1948, the West German economy grew exceptionally fast in the 1950s.
183.background: After the war, many cities lay in ruins. With the introduction of the Deutsche Mark in 1948, aid from the American Marshall Plan and the social market economy under economics minister Ludwig Erhard, a rapid upswing began. Production rose, unemployment fell almost to zero and many families could afford a fridge, television or car for the first time. Because there was a labour shortage, the Federal Republic concluded recruitment agreements with other countries from 1955, including Turkey in 1961.
183.otherOptions: The 1940s were marked by war and post-war hardship. In the 1970s the oil crisis of 1973 brought economic problems, and in the 1980s unemployment was comparatively high.
183.memoryTip: Economic miracle = 1950s, Deutsche Mark, Ludwig Erhard.

184.summary: The State of Israel was founded on the basis of a United Nations resolution.
184.whyCorrect: In November 1947, the UN General Assembly adopted a partition plan for Palestine.
184.background: On 29 November 1947, the United Nations General Assembly voted in Resolution 181 to divide what was then the British Mandate of Palestine into a Jewish and an Arab state. On 14 May 1948, David Ben-Gurion proclaimed the State of Israel. For many Holocaust survivors, Israel became a new home. The Federal Republic and Israel established diplomatic relations in 1965.
184.otherOptions: The Zionist Congress of 1897 in Basel under Theodor Herzl formulated the goal of a Jewish homeland, but was not a legal basis for founding the state. There was no federal government in 1947. The Soviet Union recognised Israel early on but did not propose its founding.

185.summary: The “Iron Curtain” stood for the Warsaw Pact sealing itself off from the West.
185.whyCorrect: It referred to the guarded border that divided Europe into East and West during the Cold War.
185.background: The term was popularised by the British politician Winston Churchill in 1946. He used it to describe how the Soviet Union and the Eastern European states it controlled sealed themselves off from the West. The Iron Curtain ran from the Baltic Sea to the Black Sea – right through Germany, where the inner-German border was secured with fences, mines and watchtowers. It fell in 1989, when Hungary opened its border and the Wall fell in the GDR.
185.otherOptions: There was never such a border between northern and southern Germany. The term has nothing to do with Nazi Germany against the Allies, and Europe was not sealed off from the USA – Western Europe and the USA were allies in the Cold War.
185.memoryTip: Iron Curtain = the border between East and West in the Cold War.

186.summary: The uprising in the GDR took place on 17 June 1953.
186.whyCorrect: In the Federal Republic, 17 June was a public holiday called the “Day of German Unity” until 1990.
186.background: On 16 and 17 June 1953, construction workers in East Berlin first protested against higher work quotas. This quickly became an uprising across the whole GDR, in which hundreds of thousands demanded free elections and the government’s resignation. Soviet tanks crushed the uprising; dozens of people were killed and thousands arrested. Since reunification, 3 October has been the Day of German Unity; in Berlin, the “Straße des 17. Juni” commemorates 17 June.
186.otherOptions: 1 May is Labour Day. The assassination attempt on Hitler took place on 20 July 1944. 9 November is the day the Wall fell in 1989 and of the pogroms in 1938.
186.memoryTip: 17 June 1953 – popular uprising in the GDR.

187.summary: The black, red and gold flag with hammer, compass and wreath of grain was the flag of the GDR.
187.whyCorrect: From 1959, the GDR flag bore the GDR’s state emblem in the centre.
187.background: The Federal Republic and the GDR both used the colours black, red and gold, which go back to the democratic movement of the 19th century. To distinguish itself, the GDR placed its emblem in the centre in 1959: the hammer stood for the workers, the compass for the intelligentsia and the wreath of grain for the farmers. This flag disappeared with reunification in 1990.
187.otherOptions: Prussia had a black and white flag. The flag of the Federal Republic is black, red and gold without a symbol. The “Third Reich” used the swastika flag.
187.memoryTip: Hammer + compass + grain = workers, intelligentsia, farmers = GDR.

188.summary: The Berlin Wall was built in 1961.
188.whyCorrect: On 13 August 1961, the GDR began sealing off the border with West Berlin.
188.background: Only two months earlier, GDR leader Walter Ulbricht had said at a press conference: “Nobody intends to build a wall.” On the night of 12–13 August 1961, soldiers and police first closed the border with barbed wire, and then the Wall was built. Families and friends were separated overnight. The Wall stood for 28 years, until 9 November 1989.
188.otherOptions: 1953 was the year of the popular uprising in the GDR. 1956 and 1959 are not significant years for the Wall.
188.memoryTip: Wall built 13 August 1961 – Wall fell 9 November 1989.

189.summary: The GDR built the Berlin Wall in 1961.
189.whyCorrect: This is the same question as question 188, just with different years.
189.background: The reason for building the Wall was mass emigration: between 1949 and 1961, around three million people had left the GDR, mainly young and well-educated people. The GDR was at risk of running out of workers. After the Wall was built, escaping was life-threatening: there was a shoot-to-kill order at the border. Nevertheless, many tried – through tunnels, by balloon or across the Baltic Sea.
189.otherOptions: In 1919 the Weimar Constitution was adopted, in 1933 the National Socialists came to power, and in 1990 Germany was reunified – by then the Wall had already fallen.

190.summary: GDR stands for German Democratic Republic (Deutsche Demokratische Republik, DDR).
190.whyCorrect: This was the name of the East German state from 1949 to 1990.
190.background: Although “democratic” was in its name, the GDR was not a democracy. The Socialist Unity Party of Germany (SED) controlled all areas of the state. Elections had only a single list, the press was censored and the state security service monitored the population. Anyone who criticised the system risked prison. Only the Peaceful Revolution of 1989 brought free elections.
190.otherOptions: “Third German Broadcasting”, “The German Republic” and “Third German Republic” are invented names.
190.memoryTip: D-D-R: Deutsche (German) – Demokratische (Democratic) – Republik (Republic) – but not a democracy.

191.summary: The Berlin Wall was opened to everyone in 1989.
191.whyCorrect: On the evening of 9 November 1989, the border crossings opened and thousands of East Berliners streamed into the West.
191.background: After mass protests and a wave of emigration via Hungary, the GDR leadership wanted to relax travel rules. At a press conference on 9 November 1989, SED politician Günter Schabowski was asked when this would apply and answered: “As far as I know … immediately, without delay.” That same evening thousands of people crowded the border crossings until the guards opened them. The images of jubilant people on the Wall went around the world.
191.otherOptions: In 1987, US President Ronald Reagan demanded in Berlin: “Tear down this wall!” – but the Wall was still standing. 1992 and 1995 were already after reunification in 1990.

192.summary: Brandenburg used to be part of the GDR.
192.whyCorrect: Brandenburg is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
192.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Brandenburg is Potsdam. Brandenburg surrounds Berlin; Sanssouci Palace is in Potsdam.
192.otherOptions: Bavaria, Saarland and Hesse were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
192.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

193.summary: From 1961 to 1989, Berlin was divided by a wall.
193.whyCorrect: The Wall separated East Berlin, the capital of the GDR, from West Berlin.
193.background: For 28 years the Wall ran right through the city and around West Berlin. It cut through streets, squares and even cemeteries. West Berliners could only travel to the East with special permits, and East Berliners were usually not allowed to go to the West at all. Today the Berlin Wall Memorial on Bernauer Straße, the East Side Gallery and a double row of cobblestones in the ground mark where the Wall ran.
193.otherOptions: Berlin always had mayors – in the West the Governing Mayor, in the East a Lord Mayor. West Berlin was not a separate state but closely tied to the Federal Republic. And West Berlin was not only reachable by plane: there were transit roads and rail connections through the GDR.

194.summary: On 3 October, Germany celebrates the Day of German Unity.
194.whyCorrect: On this day in 1990, the GDR joined the Federal Republic – Germany was reunified.
194.background: The Day of German Unity is Germany’s national holiday and a public holiday in all federal states. It commemorates reunification on 3 October 1990, made possible by the Peaceful Revolution in the GDR and the Two Plus Four Treaty with the four victorious powers. The main celebration takes place in a different state each year, usually the one currently chairing the Bundesrat.
194.otherOptions: There is no “Day of the Nation”, “Day of the Federal States” or “Day of the Cities” as a public holiday.

195.summary: Saxony-Anhalt used to be part of the GDR.
195.whyCorrect: Saxony-Anhalt is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
195.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Saxony-Anhalt is Magdeburg. In Wittenberg in Saxony-Anhalt, Martin Luther published his theses in 1517 – the start of the Reformation.
195.otherOptions: Hesse, North Rhine-Westphalia and Saarland were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
195.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

196.summary: The period in autumn 1989 is called “Die Wende” (the turning point) because the GDR changed from a dictatorship to a democracy.
196.whyCorrect: Through peaceful protests the SED lost its power; in 1990 the first free elections were held in the GDR.
196.background: In autumn 1989, hundreds of thousands demonstrated in the GDR for freedom, freedom to travel and democracy, while many fled to the West via Hungary and Czechoslovakia. In October, head of state Erich Honecker had to resign, and in November the Wall fell. On 18 March 1990, the first free elections to the People’s Chamber took place. Because everything happened without violence, it is often called the “Peaceful Revolution” today.
196.otherOptions: The GDR had not been a liberal market economy before, but socialist with a planned economy. It was never a monarchy, nor a religious state – on the contrary, religion was pushed back in the GDR.

197.summary: Thuringia used to be part of the GDR.
197.whyCorrect: Thuringia is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
197.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Thuringia is Erfurt. Goethe and Schiller lived in Weimar, and in 1919 the National Assembly met there and adopted the Weimar Constitution.
197.otherOptions: Hesse, Bavaria and Bremen were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
197.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

198.summary: Saxony used to be part of the GDR.
198.whyCorrect: Saxony is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
198.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Saxony is Dresden. The Monday demonstrations that helped bring down the Wall began in Leipzig in 1989.
198.otherOptions: Bavaria, Lower Saxony and Baden-Württemberg were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
198.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

199.summary: In the GDR, “Stasi” referred to the Ministry for State Security.
199.whyCorrect: The Stasi was the GDR’s secret police and intelligence service and monitored its own population.
199.background: The Stasi called itself the “shield and sword of the Party”. Its job was to secure the SED’s power by watching, intimidating and arresting critics. In 1989 it had around 90,000 full-time employees and many unofficial collaborators (IM) who spied on friends, colleagues and even family members. After the Peaceful Revolution the Stasi files were opened; today anyone can ask the Federal Archives whether a file exists on them.
199.otherOptions: The GDR’s parliament was called the People’s Chamber (Volkskammer), and the ruling party was the SED. The Ministry of Education was responsible for schools – it had nothing directly to do with surveillance.
199.memoryTip: Stasi = state security = the GDR’s secret police.

200.summary: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania used to be part of the GDR.
200.whyCorrect: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is one of the five eastern German states that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
200.background: The territory of the GDR included today’s states of Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia, as well as East Berlin. However, the GDR had no states: they were abolished in 1952 and replaced by 15 districts. Only in 1990 were the states re-established, and they joined the Federal Republic on 3 October. The capital of Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania is Schwerin. The state lies on the Baltic Sea and includes Rügen, Germany’s largest island.
200.otherOptions: Hesse, Schleswig-Holstein and Saarland were always in western Germany and belonged to the Federal Republic. Remember the five “new states”: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
200.memoryTip: Five new states: Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.

201.summary: Only list 2 contains nothing but former GDR states: Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia.
201.whyCorrect: These are exactly the five “new states” that joined the Federal Republic in 1990.
201.background: When it was founded, the GDR had five states, but it abolished them in 1952 and divided its territory into districts. Shortly before reunification, the states were re-established in 1990. On 3 October 1990, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia joined the Federal Republic; East Berlin was united with West Berlin to form the state of Berlin.
201.otherOptions: The other lists contain western German states: Lower Saxony, North Rhine-Westphalia, Hesse, Schleswig-Holstein, Bavaria, Baden-Württemberg and Rhineland-Palatinate always belonged to the Federal Republic. Note that a single “wrong” state in a list is enough to make it incorrect.
201.memoryTip: East list: MV, Brandenburg, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt, Thuringia – nothing else.

202.summary: In the Cold War, the GDR belonged to the Warsaw Pact.
202.whyCorrect: The Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Soviet Union and its allies in Eastern Europe.
202.background: After the Second World War, two blocs faced each other: the West with the USA and NATO, and the East with the Soviet Union. This period is called the “Cold War” because the great powers did not fight each other directly but were heavily armed. The GDR was a founding member of the Warsaw Pact in 1955; the Federal Republic joined NATO in the same year. The border between the blocs thus ran right through Germany. The Warsaw Pact was dissolved in 1991.
202.otherOptions: The Federal Republic belonged to the Western powers and NATO. Non-aligned states such as Yugoslavia or India did not want to belong to either bloc.
202.memoryTip: East = GDR = Warsaw Pact; West = Federal Republic = NATO.

203.summary: The GDR’s economic system was called a planned economy.
203.whyCorrect: The state decided in plans what was produced, how much and at what price.
203.background: In the GDR, most enterprises belonged to the state, for example as “publicly owned enterprises” (VEB). The State Planning Commission drew up five-year plans for the whole economy. Prices were fixed rather than formed on the market. This often led to shortages: many goods were scarce, and people had to wait many years for a car such as the Trabant. After reunification the enterprises were privatised, and many had to close.
203.otherOptions: Market economy, capitalism and “supply and demand” describe economic systems in which the market sets prices – this existed in the Federal Republic, not in the GDR.
203.memoryTip: GDR = planned economy; Federal Republic = social market economy.

204.summary: Today’s five eastern federal states joined the Federal Republic of Germany.
204.whyCorrect: The freely elected People’s Chamber of the GDR decided to accede to the area of application of the Basic Law as of 3 October 1990.
204.background: After the first free elections in March 1990, the Federal Republic and the GDR negotiated unification. In July 1990 the Deutsche Mark was introduced in the GDR, and in August both states signed the Unification Treaty. On 23 August 1990, the People’s Chamber decided on accession under what was then Article 23 of the Basic Law. In foreign policy, the Two Plus Four Treaty with the four victorious powers cleared the way. On 3 October 1990 Germany was reunified.
204.otherOptions: There was no occupation – neither by the Federal Republic nor by the GDR. Unity came about through a free, democratic decision by the people of the GDR. The western states did not join the GDR; it was the other way round.
204.memoryTip: Unity in 1990 = the new states joined the Federal Republic.

205.summary: With accession, the new federal states also belong to the European Union.
205.whyCorrect: Because the Federal Republic was already a member, the territory of the former GDR automatically became part of the European Community in 1990, which later became the EU.
205.background: The Federal Republic had been a member of the European Communities since the 1950s. With reunification on 3 October 1990, European law also applied in the new states – without the EU treaties having to be changed. People in eastern Germany thus became EU citizens. The European Communities became the European Union in 1993.
205.otherOptions: The Warsaw Pact was the Eastern military alliance; it dissolved in 1991, and united Germany never belonged to it. OPEC is an organisation of oil-exporting countries. The European Defence Community was a 1950s plan that never came about.
205.memoryTip: New states → Federal Republic → automatically EU.

206.summary: The “Stolpersteine” (stumbling stones) commemorate the victims of National Socialism.
206.whyCorrect: Small brass plaques in the pavement give the names and fates of people who lived there and were persecuted or murdered.
206.background: The Stolpersteine are a project by the artist Gunter Demnig, who began it in 1992. Each stone is about ten by ten centimetres and is placed in front of the victim’s last freely chosen home. It says, for example, “Here lived …”, the year of birth, the deportation and the place of death. The stones commemorate Jews, Sinti and Roma, political prisoners, homosexuals, people with disabilities and other victims. There are now well over 100,000 Stolpersteine in many European countries – the largest decentralised memorial in the world.
206.otherOptions: Famous politicians are commemorated by monuments or street names, road accident victims sometimes by roadside crosses. Jewish musicians are also honoured – but the Stolpersteine commemorate the victims of Nazi persecution.
206.memoryTip: Stumbling in your mind: a person persecuted by the Nazis lived here.

207.summary: The GDR was a member of the Warsaw Pact.
207.whyCorrect: From 1955 to 1991, the Warsaw Pact was the military alliance of the Soviet Union and the socialist states of Eastern Europe.
207.background: The Warsaw Pact was founded in 1955 as a counterpart to NATO. Besides the Soviet Union and the GDR, its members included Poland, Czechoslovakia, Hungary, Romania and Bulgaria. In 1968, Pact troops crushed the “Prague Spring” in Czechoslovakia. The GDR provided its own troops with the National People’s Army. With the end of the Cold War, the alliance dissolved in 1991; many former members are now in NATO.
207.otherOptions: The Federal Republic was in NATO. The Confederation of the Rhine was an association of German states under Napoleon from 1806. A “European Alliance” as a military alliance does not exist.

208.summary: The “Stasi” was the secret service of the GDR.
208.whyCorrect: Stasi is short for the Ministry for State Security.
208.background: The Stasi monitored millions of people: it tapped phones, opened letters, bugged flats and used informers. Anyone considered an opponent could lose their job, end up in prison or be put under psychological pressure. The former Stasi prison in Berlin-Hohenschönhausen is now a memorial. Today, those affected can read in the Stasi files who spied on them. This question is closely related to question 199.
208.otherOptions: The secret police in the “Third Reich” was called the Gestapo, not the Stasi. The Stasi was not itself a memorial – today there are memorials commemorating its victims. Nor was it a sports club.
208.memoryTip: Gestapo = Nazi secret police; Stasi = GDR secret service.

209.summary: The coat of arms of the GDR is image 4.
209.whyCorrect: It shows a hammer and compass inside a wreath of grain wrapped in a black, red and gold ribbon.
209.background: The GDR’s state emblem was meant to represent the alliance of workers (hammer), intelligentsia (compass) and farmers (wreath of grain). From 1959 it also appeared in the centre of the GDR flag. It disappeared with reunification in 1990. The same images appear in question 21 – where the question asks for the coat of arms of the Federal Republic.
209.otherOptions: Image 1 is the coat of arms of the Federal Republic of Germany with the federal eagle. Image 2 is the Chi-Rho, a Christian symbol. Image 3 is the Iron Cross, the emblem of the Bundeswehr.
209.memoryTip: Hammer and compass = GDR (image 4); eagle = Federal Republic (image 1).

210.summary: On 17 June 1953 there were nationwide strikes and a popular uprising in the GDR.
210.whyCorrect: Hundreds of thousands of people protested against the SED government; Soviet tanks crushed the uprising.
210.background: The trigger was higher work quotas: workers were expected to produce more without being paid more. Within a day, a strike by construction workers in East Berlin became an uprising in more than 700 places across the GDR. People demanded free elections and German unity. The Soviet Union declared a state of emergency and deployed tanks. Dozens of people were killed. This question is closely related to question 186.
210.otherOptions: The GDR only joined the Warsaw Pact in 1955. The SED had already been founded in 1946. Fidel Castro only visited the GDR in 1972.
210.memoryTip: 17 June 1953 = popular uprising in the GDR.

211.summary: Willy Brandt stands for the “Eastern Treaties” (Ostverträge).
211.whyCorrect: As Federal Chancellor in the early 1970s, Brandt concluded treaties with the Soviet Union, Poland, the GDR and Czechoslovakia.
211.background: Willy Brandt (SPD) was Federal Chancellor from 1969 to 1974. With his “New Ostpolitik”, he wanted to improve relations with the Eastern Bloc states – following the motto “change through rapprochement”. With the Moscow and Warsaw Treaties of 1970, the Federal Republic recognised the existing borders in Europe, including the Oder–Neisse border with Poland. The Basic Treaty with the GDR followed in 1972. Brandt received the Nobel Peace Prize in 1971 for this policy.
211.otherOptions: Helmut Kohl was the “Chancellor of Unity” (1982–1998). Mikhail Gorbachev was the Soviet leader who introduced reforms. Ludwig Erhard is regarded as the father of the economic miracle.
211.memoryTip: Brandt = Ostpolitik, the genuflection, Nobel Peace Prize.

212.summary: Germany’s full name is the Federal Republic of Germany (Bundesrepublik Deutschland).
212.whyCorrect: This is how it appears in the Basic Law; the international country code is DE.
212.background: The name already says a lot about the state: “Bund” (federal) stands for the federal state of 16 states, “Republik” for an elected head of state instead of a king. Article 20 of the Basic Law begins: “The Federal Republic of Germany is a democratic and social federal state.” The name has applied since the founding in 1949 and remained the same after reunification in 1990.
212.otherOptions: “Federal State of Germany”, “Federal States of Germany” and “Federal District of Germany” are not official names. “Federal state” does describe the form of the state, but it is not the name.
212.memoryTip: Federal + Republic = Federal Republic of Germany.

213.whyCorrect: This makes Germany the most populous country in the European Union.
213.background: According to the Federal Statistical Office, just under 84 million people live in Germany. The most populous federal state is North Rhine-Westphalia with around 18 million inhabitants, and the largest city is Berlin with almost four million. Germany is a country of immigration: around a quarter of the population has an immigration history, meaning they themselves or both parents immigrated to Germany since 1950.
213.otherOptions: 70 and 78 million are too few, 90 million too many. Before reunification, the Federal Republic had around 63 million and the GDR around 16 million inhabitants.
213.memoryTip: Germany: about 84 million – the most in the EU.

214.summary: The German flag is black, red and gold.
214.whyCorrect: Article 22 of the Basic Law states: “The federal flag shall be black, red and gold.”
214.background: The colours black, red and gold stand for the 19th-century movement for freedom and unity. They go back to the uniforms of the Lützow Free Corps in the wars of liberation against Napoleon and became the symbol of a democratic, united Germany at the Hambach Festival in 1832 and in the revolution of 1848. The Weimar Republic also used these colours. The National Socialists abolished them – the Federal Republic deliberately reintroduced them in 1949.
214.otherOptions: Black, white and red were the colours of the German Empire; the National Socialists also used them. Black, yellow and red is the flag of Belgium. Black, red and green is not a German flag.
214.memoryTip: Black-red-gold = democracy and unity (1848, Weimar, Federal Republic).

215.summary: Helmut Kohl is known as the “Chancellor of German Unity”.
215.whyCorrect: Helmut Kohl (CDU) was Federal Chancellor in 1989/90 and played a decisive role in driving reunification forward.
215.background: Helmut Kohl was Federal Chancellor from 1982 to 1998 – 16 years, longer than any other chancellor. After the fall of the Wall, he presented a ten-point programme for German unity in November 1989. He negotiated with the USA, the Soviet Union under Mikhail Gorbachev, Britain and France until the Two Plus Four Treaty made unity possible in 1990. Together with French President François Mitterrand, he also advanced European integration and the introduction of the euro.
215.otherOptions: Gerhard Schröder (1998–2005) was Kohl’s successor. Konrad Adenauer was the first Chancellor (1949–1963), and Helmut Schmidt was Chancellor from 1974 to 1982.

216.summary: The federal eagle can be seen in the plenary chamber of the Bundestag.
216.whyCorrect: A large eagle sculpture hangs on the front wall behind the speaker’s lectern and the seats of the Presidium.
216.background: The eagle in the plenary chamber is based on a design by the sculptor Ludwig Gies, originally created for the Bundestag in Bonn. For the move to Berlin, it was redesigned in a larger form in the Reichstag building. Because of its round shape, people affectionately call it the “fat hen”. The federal eagle is the state symbol of the Federal Republic and stands for the democracy represented in the Bundestag.
216.otherOptions: The flag of the city of Berlin with the bear does not hang in the plenary chamber. The imperial eagle (Reichsadler) was the symbol of the German Empire and the Weimar Republic. The Imperial Crown is the crown of the medieval Holy Roman Empire and is kept in Vienna today.

217.whyCorrect: It was founded on 7 October 1949 and joined the Federal Republic on 3 October 1990.
217.background: The German Democratic Republic existed for almost 41 years. It emerged in the Soviet occupation zone and was ruled by the SED. In 1961 it built the Wall, and in 1989 peaceful protests brought about the turning point (“Wende”). With reunification on 3 October 1990, the GDR ceased to exist.
217.otherOptions: 1919 to 1927 falls within the Weimar Republic, and 1933 to 1945 was the Nazi dictatorship. 1945 to 1961 is wrong, because there was no GDR yet in 1945, and in 1961 the Wall was built – the GDR existed for almost 30 more years after that.

218.summary: With reunification in 1990, five federal states joined the Federal Republic.
218.whyCorrect: These were Brandenburg, Mecklenburg-Western Pomerania, Saxony, Saxony-Anhalt and Thuringia.
218.background: Before 1990, the Federal Republic had ten states, plus West Berlin with a special status. With unification the five new states joined, and East and West Berlin were united to form the state of Berlin. Since then there have been 16 federal states. Berlin is therefore not counted as a “new” state but as a state that was put back together.
218.otherOptions: Four, six or seven are wrong. Anyone who counts six includes Berlin – but half of Berlin (West Berlin) was already closely tied to the Federal Republic before.

219.summary: The Federal Republic of Germany has had its current borders since 1990.
219.whyCorrect: With reunification and the Two Plus Four Treaty, the borders of united Germany were finally settled.
219.background: In the Two Plus Four Treaty of September 1990, the Federal Republic, the GDR and the four victorious powers agreed that united Germany would consist of the territory of the two German states and all of Berlin. In November 1990, the German–Polish Border Treaty finally confirmed the Oder–Neisse border. Germany thus renounced all territorial claims. Since then, Germany has had nine neighbouring countries.
219.otherOptions: In 1933 Germany still included territories in the east that now belong to Poland and Russia. In 1949 the Federal Republic was founded, but without the GDR – and without Saarland, which only joined in 1957. In 1971 the Four Power Agreement on Berlin was concluded; it did not change any borders.

220.summary: 27 January commemorates the victims of National Socialism – it is the anniversary of the liberation of the Auschwitz extermination camp.
220.whyCorrect: On 27 January 1945, Soviet soldiers liberated the survivors of the Auschwitz-Birkenau camp.
220.background: Auschwitz-Birkenau in occupied Poland was the largest Nazi extermination camp. More than one million people were murdered there, most of them Jews. In 1996, Federal President Roman Herzog declared 27 January a day of remembrance for the victims of National Socialism. Since 2005 it has also been the United Nations’ International Holocaust Remembrance Day. Every year on this day the Bundestag holds a commemoration.
220.otherOptions: The end of the Second World War in Europe was on 8 May 1945, the promulgation of the Basic Law on 23 May 1949 and reunification on 3 October 1990.
220.memoryTip: 27 January = Auschwitz liberated = Holocaust Remembrance Day.

221.summary: Schengen means: Germans can travel to many European countries without passport checks.
221.whyCorrect: Between Schengen states there are generally no regular checks at internal borders.
221.background: The Schengen Agreement was signed in 1985 in the Luxembourg village of Schengen. Today 29 states belong to the Schengen Area, most EU countries as well as Norway, Iceland, Switzerland and Liechtenstein. When travelling between these countries, you normally do not have to stop at the border. You should still always carry an ID document, because states may temporarily reintroduce border checks – Germany currently does so at several borders.
221.otherOptions: Not everyone can enter Germany without checks: there are checks at the Schengen Area’s external borders, and many people need a visa. Travelling to every country in the world without passport checks is not possible. And the euro is not legal tender in every country – that has nothing to do with Schengen.

222.summary: Switzerland is a neighbouring country of Germany.
222.whyCorrect: Germany borders Switzerland in the south, including at Lake Constance and the High Rhine.
222.background: Germany has nine neighbouring countries – more than any other country in Europe: Denmark to the north, Poland and the Czech Republic to the east, Austria and Switzerland to the south and France, Luxembourg, Belgium and the Netherlands to the west. In Switzerland, German is one of the official languages and is spoken by the majority of the population. Switzerland is not an EU member but belongs to the Schengen Area.
222.otherOptions: Hungary lies beyond Austria and does not border Germany. Portugal and Spain are on the Iberian Peninsula in south-western Europe – France lies in between.
222.memoryTip: Nine neighbours: DK, PL, CZ, AT, CH, FR, LU, BE, NL.

223.summary: Poland is a neighbouring country of Germany.
223.whyCorrect: The German–Polish border runs in the east along the rivers Oder and Neisse.
223.background: The border with Poland is about 470 kilometres long. After the Second World War it was set along the Oder and Neisse; the Federal Republic recognised it in the Treaty of Warsaw in 1970, and united Germany finally in 1990. Today both countries are members of the EU and NATO, and the border is open. Many people commute daily between towns such as Frankfurt (Oder) and Słubice or Görlitz and Zgorzelec.
223.otherOptions: Romania, Bulgaria and Greece are in south-eastern Europe and do not border Germany. Like Germany, however, they are members of the European Union.
223.memoryTip: East: Poland and the Czech Republic are neighbours.

224.summary: EU is short for European Union.
224.whyCorrect: The EU is an association of 27 European states.
224.background: The European Union was formed in 1993 from the European Communities, which Germany co-founded in the 1950s. The EU states share a single market in which goods, services, capital and people can move freely. Important institutions are the European Parliament, which citizens elect directly, the European Commission in Brussels and the Court of Justice of the European Union in Luxembourg. 21 of the 27 countries use the euro as their currency; Bulgaria joined most recently in 2026.
224.otherOptions: “European Enterprises”, “Unified Union” and “Euro Union” are invented terms. The euro is the currency of many EU countries, but not the name of the Union.

225.summary: Austria has a large German-speaking population.
225.whyCorrect: In Austria, German is the official language and the mother tongue of the vast majority.
225.background: German is an official language not only in Germany but also in Austria, Liechtenstein and – alongside other languages – in Switzerland, Luxembourg and Belgium. In Italy it is a regional official language in South Tyrol. In total, around 100 million people in Europe speak German as their mother tongue, making it the most widely spoken mother tongue in the EU. Austrian German has some words of its own, such as “Jänner” for January or “Paradeiser” for tomato.
225.otherOptions: The Czech Republic has only a small German minority. Some Germans do live in Norway and Spain, for example retirees on Mallorca, but there is no large German-speaking population there.
225.memoryTip: German as an official language: Germany, Austria, Switzerland, Liechtenstein, Luxembourg, Belgium.

226.summary: The flag of the European Union is image 2.
226.whyCorrect: It shows a circle of twelve golden stars on a blue background.
226.background: The twelve stars do not represent the number of member states but unity, perfection and harmony – which is why the number always stays the same, even when new countries join. The flag was introduced by the Council of Europe in 1955 and has also been used by the European Communities since 1986 and today by the EU. In Germany it often flies next to the federal flag on public buildings.
226.otherOptions: Image 1 is the flag of the USA with stars and stripes. Image 3 is the flag of the United Nations with the world map. Image 4 is the flag of the Commonwealth of Independent States (CIS), an association of several former Soviet republics.
226.memoryTip: EU = twelve golden stars in a circle on blue.

227.summary: Denmark is a neighbouring country of Germany.
227.whyCorrect: Denmark shares a border with Germany.
227.background: Denmark is Germany’s only neighbour to the north. The border is in Schleswig-Holstein, for example near Flensburg. Minorities live on both sides: Danes in Germany and Germans in Denmark. The party of the Danish minority, the SSW, is exempt from the 5 percent threshold. In total, Germany has nine neighbouring countries.
227.otherOptions: Finland, Norway and Sweden are also in the north, but on the other side of the Baltic Sea – they have no land border with Germany.
227.memoryTip: Only one neighbour to the north: Denmark.

228.summary: The GDR’s accession to the Federal Republic in 1990 is called German reunification.
228.whyCorrect: After more than 40 years of division, the two German states became one state again on 3 October 1990.
228.background: The term reunification describes the coming together of what had been separated after the Second World War. It was made possible by the Peaceful Revolution in the GDR, the fall of the Wall and the consent of the four victorious powers in the Two Plus Four Treaty. People also speak of “German Unity”. That is why 3 October is a national holiday.
228.otherOptions: NATO’s eastward enlargement began in 1999, when former Eastern Bloc states such as Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary joined NATO. The EU’s eastward enlargement took place in 2004, when ten states – most of them from Central and Eastern Europe – joined the EU. The European Community was the forerunner of the EU.

229.summary: Luxembourg is a neighbouring country of Germany.
229.whyCorrect: Luxembourg shares a border with Germany.
229.background: Luxembourg borders Rhineland-Palatinate and Saarland in the west. The small Grand Duchy is one of the founding states of the European Communities, and the city of Luxembourg hosts important EU institutions such as the Court of Justice. German is an official language there alongside Luxembourgish and French. Many people commute daily from Germany to work in Luxembourg.
229.otherOptions: Spain lies in south-western Europe beyond France, Bulgaria in the south-east and Norway in the north beyond the Baltic Sea – none of them borders Germany.
229.memoryTip: In the west: France, Luxembourg, Belgium, the Netherlands.

230.summary: The European Parliament is elected every five years.
230.whyCorrect: The last European election was in June 2024; the next is in 2029.
230.background: In the European election, citizens of all 27 EU states elect their members of the European Parliament. It currently has 720 members in total; Germany, with 96, has the most. In Germany, 16-year-olds have been able to vote since 2024, as can all EU citizens living here. Together with the Council of the EU, the Parliament adopts European laws and the EU budget.
230.otherOptions: Six, seven or eight years are wrong. Five years also applies to most state parliaments and to the Federal President’s term; the Bundestag is elected every four years.

231.summary: “European integration” means the coming together of European states to form the EU.
231.whyCorrect: It refers to the gradual process in which European states cooperate ever more closely.
231.background: European integration began after the Second World War with the aim of securing peace. In 1951, six states founded the Coal and Steel Community, and in 1957 the European Economic Community. Later came the single market, the Schengen Area without border checks and the euro. At the same time, the community grew from six to 27 members today. People speak of “deepening” (more cooperation) and “widening” (more members).
231.otherOptions: Immigrants from America, an immigration stop or European emigrants in the USA have nothing to do with the term. Here “integration” means states growing together, not individual people.

232.summary: In the European election, the members of the European Parliament are elected.
232.whyCorrect: The European Parliament is the only EU institution elected directly by citizens.
232.background: Members of the European Parliament work together in political groups formed by political orientation, not by country. Together with the Council of the EU (the governments of the member states), the Parliament adopts laws, decides on the budget and confirms the European Commission. In Germany there is no 5 percent threshold for the European election, so smaller parties are also represented.
232.otherOptions: The European Commission is not elected directly: the governments propose it, and Parliament must approve it. The EU states decide together on the accession of new countries, not the voters. A European constitution was rejected in referendums in 2005; the Treaty of Lisbon applies instead.
232.memoryTip: European election = election of the European Parliament.

233.summary: The Czech Republic is a neighbouring country of Germany.
233.whyCorrect: The Czech Republic shares a border with Germany.
233.background: The Czech Republic borders Bavaria and Saxony in the south-east; the border runs through the Ore Mountains and the Bavarian Forest, among other places. The capital, Prague, is about two hours from Dresden. The Czech Republic has been an EU member since 2004 and belongs to the Schengen Area. In the past there was a large German-speaking population in Bohemia, which was expelled after 1945.
233.otherOptions: Bulgaria, Greece and Portugal lie further away in southern and south-eastern Europe and have no border with Germany.
233.memoryTip: In the east: Poland and the Czech Republic.

234.summary: Strasbourg is one of the seats of the European Parliament.
234.whyCorrect: Most plenary sessions of the European Parliament take place in Strasbourg, France.
234.background: The European Parliament has three places of work. Its official seat is Strasbourg, where Parliament meets twelve times a year for plenary sessions lasting several days. Committees and political groups meet in Brussels, where there are also additional plenary sessions. The General Secretariat, i.e. the administration, works in Luxembourg. Strasbourg is in Alsace, right on the German border – a symbol of Franco-German reconciliation.
234.otherOptions: London is the capital of the United Kingdom, which left the EU in 2020. Paris and Berlin are capitals of member states but not seats of the European Parliament.

235.summary: The meeting at Verdun shows the EU’s aim of peace and security among its member states.
235.whyCorrect: Former wartime enemies jointly commemorate the dead and show that enemies have become partners.
235.background: On 22 September 1984, Federal Chancellor Helmut Kohl and President François Mitterrand stood in front of a military cemetery near Verdun and held hands. Hundreds of thousands of German and French soldiers had died in the Battle of Verdun in 1916. The image became a symbol of Franco-German friendship, which is the engine of European unification. The EU was created precisely to make war between its members impossible; in 2012 it received the Nobel Peace Prize for this.
235.otherOptions: England does not appear in this picture – it is about Germany and France. Freedom of travel and common public holidays are not the subject of a commemoration of war dead.
235.memoryTip: Verdun 1984: Kohl + Mitterrand hand in hand = peace in Europe.

236.summary: The EU has 27 member states today.
236.whyCorrect: There have been 27 since the United Kingdom left on 31 January 2020.
236.background: The European Community began in 1957 with six states. More joined over time; the biggest enlargement was in 2004 with ten new countries, and the most recent member was Croatia in 2013 as the 28th state. With Brexit, the United Kingdom became the first country to leave the EU. Several countries, such as those in the Western Balkans as well as Ukraine and Moldova, are candidates for membership.
236.otherOptions: 21, 23 and 25 are wrong. The EU had 25 members from 2004 to 2007, before Bulgaria and Romania joined.

237.summary: The Treaties of Rome founded the European Economic Community (EEC).
237.whyCorrect: The treaties were signed in Rome on 25 March 1957 and are regarded as the birth of today’s EU.
237.background: In 1957, Belgium, the Federal Republic of Germany, France, Italy, Luxembourg and the Netherlands signed two treaties in Rome: one founded the European Economic Community with the goal of a common market, the other the European Atomic Energy Community (Euratom). The treaties entered into force in 1958. Customs duties between the members were gradually abolished. In 2007, the EU celebrated the 50th anniversary with the “Berlin Declaration”.
237.otherOptions: The Federal Republic joined NATO in 1955 – this was arranged by the Paris Agreements. Reparations and the Oder–Neisse border were not part of the Treaties of Rome; united Germany finally recognised the Oder–Neisse border in 1990.
237.memoryTip: Rome 1957 = EEC = the beginning of the EU.

238.summary: The European Parliament works in Strasbourg, Luxembourg and Brussels.
238.whyCorrect: Strasbourg is the official seat for plenary sessions, Brussels the place for committees and Luxembourg the seat of the administration.
238.background: The fact that Parliament works in three places is set out in the EU treaties and is a compromise between the member states. For the members, this means a lot of travel: every month, Parliament moves from Brussels to Strasbourg for a session week. This is repeatedly debated, but any change would have to be agreed unanimously by all member states. This question is closely related to question 234.
238.otherOptions: Paris, London, The Hague, Rome, Bern, Vienna, Bonn, Zurich and Milan are not places of work of the European Parliament. Bern and Zurich are in Switzerland, which is not an EU member at all; London is in the United Kingdom, which has left the EU.

239.summary: The Federal Republic joined other states to form the European Economic Community through the Treaties of Rome.
239.whyCorrect: The Treaties of Rome of 1957 founded the EEC and Euratom.
239.background: The Treaties of Rome were a major step in European unification: instead of only cooperating on coal and steel, the six founding states created a common market for all goods. The EEC later became the European Community (EC) and in 1993, with the Maastricht Treaty, the European Union. Federal Chancellor Konrad Adenauer signed the treaties for the Federal Republic. See also question 237.
239.otherOptions: “Paris Treaties” is a trap: the Coal and Steel Community was founded in Paris in 1951, and the Paris Agreements of 1954 arranged the Federal Republic’s accession to NATO – but the EEC was founded in Rome. “Hamburg” and “London Treaties” have nothing to do with the EEC.
239.memoryTip: EEC = Rome (1957). Coal and steel = Paris (1951).

240.summary: Cash payments in euros have been made in Germany since 2002.
240.whyCorrect: On 1 January 2002, euro banknotes and coins were introduced and replaced the Deutsche Mark.
240.background: As book money, for example for bank transfers, the euro had already existed since 1 January 1999. Cash followed three years later. The exchange rate was fixed: 1 euro equalled 1.95583 Deutsche Marks. That is why many people kept “dividing by two” for a long time. Deutsche Mark notes and coins can still be exchanged at the Deutsche Bundesbank with no time limit.
240.otherOptions: In 1995 and 1998 the euro did not yet exist as cash; in 1995, however, the name “euro” was decided. By 2005, people had already been paying with euros for three years.

241.summary: To receive parental allowance (Elterngeld), Ms Seger must submit an application to the parental allowance office.
241.whyCorrect: Parental allowance is only paid on application; the parental allowance office of the federal state or municipality is responsible.
241.background: Parental allowance replaces part of income when parents work less or not at all after the birth in order to look after their child. It usually amounts to 65 to 67 percent of previous net income, at least 300 and at most 1,800 euros a month. Parents can receive it for up to 14 months together. You apply after the birth, in many states also online. Important: parental allowance is only paid retroactively for three months – so you should not apply too late.
241.otherOptions: During maternity protection, the health insurance fund pays maternity benefit, but not parental allowance. Parental allowance is not paid automatically. And the employment office does not have to give permission – parental leave is requested from the employer.
241.memoryTip: Parental allowance = apply to the parental allowance office, not too late.

242.summary: Whether a child goes to nursery (Kindergarten) is decided by the parents or legal guardians.
242.whyCorrect: In Germany, nursery is generally voluntary – unlike school.
242.background: Since 2013, every child from their first birthday has had a legal right to a place in a day-care centre or with a childminder. But whether the family uses this place is up to the parents. Many parents send their children to nursery because they play with other children there, learn German and are prepared for school. Costs vary from state to state; in some states nursery is entirely or partly free of charge.
242.otherOptions: The state and the federal states ensure there are enough places, but generally do not make attendance compulsory. Schools are only responsible once compulsory schooling begins.
242.memoryTip: School = compulsory; nursery = the parents’ decision.

243.summary: A street demonstration must be registered in advance.
243.whyCorrect: Open-air assemblies must usually be registered with the competent authority at least 48 hours before they are announced.
243.background: Article 8 of the Basic Law guarantees all Germans the right to assemble peacefully and unarmed – “without prior notification or permission”. For open-air assemblies, however, the law can require registration, and it does. Important: registration is not a request for permission. The authority mainly has to manage traffic and ensure safety. A demonstration can only be banned in exceptional cases, for example if there is an immediate danger to public safety. Spontaneous demonstrations are also possible.
243.otherOptions: You cannot demonstrate “anywhere at any time” without doing anything – on the street, registration is needed. Demonstrations are not forbidden in Germany; they are a fundamental right. And you do not have to found an association: anyone may register a demonstration.
243.memoryTip: Demonstrating is a right – but outdoors, register first.

244.summary: To start studying at a university, you normally need the Abitur.
244.whyCorrect: The Abitur is the general higher education entrance qualification and entitles you to study at all universities.
244.background: The Abitur is usually taken after 12 or 13 years of school at a grammar school (Gymnasium) or comprehensive school. But there are other routes to higher education: with the Fachhochschulreife you can study at universities of applied sciences, and people with vocational qualifications – for example a master craftsman’s certificate or after training and work experience – can also begin a degree. Foreign school qualifications are assessed and may be recognised.
244.otherOptions: A Diplom is a university degree you receive at the end of your studies, not before. Prokura is a commercial power of attorney for company employees. The journeyman’s examination (Gesellenprüfung) completes an apprenticeship in a skilled trade.

245.summary: Anne (13) and Tim (25) may not live together as a couple.
245.whyCorrect: Anne is a child; sexual acts with children under 14 are strictly forbidden in Germany.
245.background: Criminal law gives special protection to children under 14: sexual acts with them are always a criminal offence, even if the child seems to agree (Section 176 of the Criminal Code). A child cannot enter into a romantic relationship with an adult. Young people between 14 and 18 are also specially protected by law. Since 2017, people in Germany may generally only marry from the age of 18.
245.otherOptions: Hans and Marie are both adults. Tom and Klaus are a same-sex couple – that is allowed, and since 2017 they can also marry. Sofie and Lisa are adults too. An age difference between adults does not matter.
245.memoryTip: Adults may live together freely – children under 14 are protected.

246.summary: In Germany you come of age at 18.
246.whyCorrect: At 18 you have full legal capacity and all the rights and duties of an adult.
246.background: Being of age means, for example, that you can sign contracts, rent a flat, marry, drive a car alone with a licence and vote in federal elections without your parents’ consent. But you are also fully responsible yourself, for instance for debts. The age of majority in Germany has been 18 since 1975; before that it was 21. Young people between 14 and 18 already have some rights, for example choosing their religion from 14.
246.otherOptions: 16 is, for example, the age for a moped licence or, in some states, for local and state elections, but not the age of majority. 19 has no special role, and 21 was the age of majority only until 1975.

247.summary: The special protection for women shortly before and after giving birth is called maternity protection (Mutterschutz).
247.whyCorrect: The Maternity Protection Act protects the health of mother and child and secures the job.
247.background: The maternity protection period begins six weeks before the expected due date and usually ends eight weeks after the birth, or twelve weeks after premature or multiple births. Before the birth, the woman may work if she expressly wishes to; after the birth there is a ban on employment. During this time she receives maternity benefit from the health insurance fund and a supplement from her employer. In addition, she generally may not be dismissed during pregnancy and up to four months after the birth.
247.otherOptions: Parental leave (Elternzeit) is time off work for mothers and fathers until the child’s third birthday. Birth preparation is a course for expectant parents, and the “Wochenbett” is the weeks of physical recovery after the birth – neither is legal protection.
247.memoryTip: Maternity protection: 6 weeks before, 8 weeks after the birth.

248.summary: In Germany, raising children is primarily the task of the parents.
248.whyCorrect: Article 6 of the Basic Law calls the care and upbringing of children “the natural right of parents and a duty primarily incumbent upon them”.
248.background: Parents decide how to raise their children – for example regarding religion, nursery or leisure. But they are also responsible for their children’s well-being. The state watches over this to make sure the child’s welfare is not at risk: in cases of neglect or violence, the youth welfare office can intervene. Since 2000, children have had an explicit right to an upbringing free of violence. Schools have their own educational mission but do not replace parents.
248.otherOptions: The state only has a guardian role: it intervenes when the child’s welfare is at risk but does not raise children in place of the parents. Grandparents can help but do not have the main responsibility. Schools teach and help with upbringing, but raising children remains primarily the parents’ job.
248.memoryTip: Upbringing: parents first – the state only watches over it.

249.summary: In Germany, raising children is primarily the task of the parents.
249.whyCorrect: Article 6 of the Basic Law calls the care and upbringing of children “the natural right of parents and a duty primarily incumbent upon them”.
249.background: Parents decide how to raise their children – for example regarding religion, nursery or leisure. But they are also responsible for their children’s well-being. The state watches over this to make sure the child’s welfare is not at risk: in cases of neglect or violence, the youth welfare office can intervene. Since 2000, children have had an explicit right to an upbringing free of violence. Schools have their own educational mission but do not replace parents. This question is almost the same as question 248.
249.otherOptions: The state, relatives and schools support parents but are not mainly responsible. The state only intervenes when the child’s welfare is at risk.
249.memoryTip: Upbringing: parents first – the state only watches over it.

250.summary: You have the best chance of a well-paid job if you are well educated and trained.
250.whyCorrect: In Germany, qualifications such as vocational training, university studies and work experience count most.
250.background: Germany has a special training system: dual vocational training, in which you work in a company while attending vocational school. There are also university degrees and further training, for example to become a master craftsman or technician. Well-trained people find work more easily and earn more on average. For immigrants it is worth having foreign qualifications recognised – advice is available, for example, through the portal “Recognition in Germany”.
250.otherOptions: Religion, gender or party membership must play no role in hiring; discrimination is prohibited by the Basic Law and the General Equal Treatment Act. On average, women still even earn somewhat less than men.

251.summary: Anyone who hits a child can be punished for it.
251.whyCorrect: In Germany, children have a right to an upbringing free of violence; hitting is forbidden.
251.background: Since 2000, the Civil Code has stated: “Children have a right to an upbringing free of violence. Corporal punishment, psychological injury and other degrading measures are inadmissible” (Section 1631 BGB). Anyone who hits a child can be prosecuted for bodily harm. This also applies to parents. The youth welfare office can intervene and support the family; if a child is in danger, it can also take the child into temporary care.
251.otherOptions: Violence against children is not a private family matter. Neighbours, teachers or doctors can and should contact the youth welfare office if they are worried. It is wrong that you cannot be punished for it.

252.summary: In Germany, you may only be married to one person at a time.
252.whyCorrect: Being married to two people (bigamy) is forbidden and a criminal offence.
252.background: German marriage law only recognises marriage between two people. Anyone who is already married and marries again commits a criminal offence under Section 172 of the Criminal Code; the second marriage can also be annulled. Since 2017, two men or two women may also marry. Germany generally does not recognise polygamous marriages concluded abroad as equivalent marriages either.
252.otherOptions: Several spouses at the same time are forbidden. After a divorce or the death of a spouse, you may of course marry again – this applies equally to women and men.

253.summary: After moving, you must register at the residents’ registration office (Einwohnermeldeamt).
253.whyCorrect: Registration must take place within two weeks of moving in; in many cities the office is now called the citizens’ office (Bürgeramt).
253.background: Germany has a registration requirement: anyone moving into a new home must register with the registration authority within two weeks (Section 17 of the Federal Registration Act). You need an ID document and a confirmation from your landlord. After registering, you receive a registration certificate, which you often need for banks, employers or authorities. Anyone who does not register can be fined. In many cities you can book an appointment online.
253.otherOptions: The registry office (Standesamt) is responsible for births, marriages and deaths. The public order office deals with public order, and the trade office with registering a business.
253.memoryTip: Moving → two weeks → residents’ registration office (Bürgeramt).

254.summary: The separation year means: the spouses live their own separate lives for at least one year; after that, divorce is possible.
254.whyCorrect: After one year of separation, the law assumes the marriage has broken down if both want a divorce.
254.background: A marriage can be dissolved if it has broken down (Section 1565 BGB). To prevent couples from acting hastily, the law generally requires a separation year. You can also live separately in the same flat if you keep separate finances and sleep apart. If both agree to the divorce, one year is enough; if one does not, the marriage is deemed to have broken down after three years of separation. Only in special cases of hardship, such as violence, is an earlier divorce possible. The family court decides on the divorce.
254.otherOptions: How long the court proceedings take depends on the individual case. How long you were married plays no role in the separation year. Contact rights for the children are not limited to one year.
254.memoryTip: First live apart for a year – then divorce.

255.summary: Parents can get help with upbringing problems from the youth welfare office (Jugendamt).
255.whyCorrect: The youth welfare office advises families free of charge and supports them with difficulties in raising children.
255.background: Every town and district has a youth welfare office. It offers parenting advice, arranges family support and helps, for example, single parents or families in crisis. Advice is free and confidential. Parenting advice centres run by welfare organisations such as Caritas, Diakonie or AWO can also help. The youth welfare office also has the task of protecting children when their welfare is at risk. Many parents are afraid of the Jugendamt – yet its most important task is to help families.
255.otherOptions: The public order office deals with public order, the school authority with supervising schools and the health office with health protection and hygiene. For questions about upbringing, the youth welfare office is the right contact.

256.summary: To open a restaurant you need a restaurant licence (Gaststättenerlaubnis) from the competent authority.
256.whyCorrect: The licence is usually issued by the town or municipality, for example the trade office or public order office.
256.background: Anyone running a restaurant is responsible for guests, neighbours and food. That is why the authority checks in advance, for example, whether the operator is reliable and whether the premises are suitable. There are further steps: registering the business, an instruction session at the health office for everyone who works with food, and compliance with hygiene rules, which food inspectors check. The exact rules differ from state to state.
256.otherOptions: The police do not issue licences for restaurants. Parties have nothing to do with permits for businesses. The residents’ registration office is responsible for registering your address, not businesses.

257.summary: An adult woman can take the Abitur later at an evening grammar school (Abendgymnasium).
257.whyCorrect: Evening grammar schools are schools for adults who want to obtain the Abitur alongside their job.
257.background: At an evening grammar school, lessons usually take place in the evening so that students can keep working during the day. Those who want to focus fully on school can attend a “Kolleg”, where classes are held during the day. The requirement is usually completed vocational training or several years of work experience. State evening grammar schools and Kollegs charge no school fees, and under certain conditions students can receive BAföG funding. So it is never too late for a higher school qualification.
257.otherOptions: You can only study at a university or private university after the Abitur – you cannot take it there. The Hauptschule leads to the lower secondary certificate, not the Abitur.
257.memoryTip: Catching up on the Abitur: evening grammar school (evenings) or Kolleg (daytime).

258.summary: The youth welfare office can remove a child who is being beaten or starved from the family.
258.whyCorrect: If a child’s welfare is in urgent danger, the youth welfare office may take the child into care.
258.background: The youth welfare office should first help families, for example with advice or a family support worker. But if a child is in acute danger – for example from violence, neglect or hunger – it may take the child into temporary care and place them with foster parents or in a facility (Section 42 of Social Code Book VIII). The family court then decides on any longer-term withdrawal of custody. Children and young people in need can also contact the youth welfare office themselves.
258.otherOptions: Parents decide which school a child attends, within the school laws. Child benefit is paid by the Family Benefits Office of the Federal Employment Agency. And whether a child attends nursery is voluntary – the youth welfare office does not check this.
258.memoryTip: Youth welfare office: help – and protect the child in an emergency.

259.summary: The Career Information Centre (BIZ) helps with finding an apprenticeship.
259.whyCorrect: At the BIZ of the employment agency, you can get free information about careers, vocational training and degree programmes.
259.background: Career Information Centres exist at employment agencies throughout Germany. They offer information on hundreds of apprenticeship occupations, application tips, computers for job searches and events. The agency’s career guidance service helps young people and adults find a suitable training place. An apprenticeship (Lehrstelle) is a training place in the dual system – in a company and at vocational school.
259.otherOptions: The German Pension Insurance helps with calculating pensions, and the tax office, an income tax assistance association or a tax adviser helps with tax returns. The health insurance fund answers questions about health insurance.
259.memoryTip: BIZ = get to know careers, find an apprenticeship.

260.summary: At school, a child is obliged to attend.
260.whyCorrect: Because of compulsory schooling, pupils must attend lessons regularly.
260.background: Compulsory schooling does not just mean being enrolled at a school, but actually going. A child who is ill must be excused, usually by the parents and, for longer illnesses, with a doctor’s certificate. Exemptions can be requested for special occasions. Unexcused absence violates compulsory schooling; parents may face a fine, and in extreme cases the police can take a child to school.
260.otherOptions: There is no unlimited free time during school. Most subjects are compulsory; choices are only possible in some areas. And “Schulgeld” is a fee you pay – state schools in Germany are free of charge, so you do not receive school money.
260.memoryTip: Compulsory schooling = going to school, not just being enrolled.

261.summary: A 30-year-old man can take the Abitur later at an evening grammar school (Abendgymnasium).
261.whyCorrect: Evening grammar schools are schools for adults who want to obtain the Abitur alongside their job.
261.background: At an evening grammar school, lessons usually take place in the evening so that students can keep working during the day. Those who want to focus fully on school can attend a “Kolleg”, where classes are held during the day. The requirement is usually completed vocational training or several years of work experience. State evening grammar schools and Kollegs charge no school fees, and under certain conditions students can receive BAföG funding. So it is never too late for a higher school qualification. This question is almost the same as question 257.
261.otherOptions: You can only study at a university or private university after the Abitur – you cannot take it there. The Hauptschule leads to the lower secondary certificate, not the Abitur.
261.memoryTip: Catching up on the Abitur: evening grammar school (evenings) or Kolleg (daytime).

262.summary: Equal treatment means: nobody may be disadvantaged, for example, because of a disability.
262.whyCorrect: Article 3 of the Basic Law prohibits discrimination on grounds including sex, origin, religion and disability.
262.background: Since 1994, the Basic Law has stated explicitly: “No person shall be disfavoured because of disability.” The General Equal Treatment Act (AGG) of 2006 also protects against discrimination at work and in everyday life – for example when looking for a flat or in a restaurant – on grounds of ethnic origin, sex, religion, disability, age or sexual identity. Anyone who is discriminated against can take action, for example with the help of the Federal Anti-Discrimination Agency, and claim compensation.
262.otherOptions: Personal reasons do not justify discrimination. On the contrary, anyone who has been discriminated against may take legal action. There is no legal obligation to donate money to disadvantaged groups every year.
262.memoryTip: Equal treatment = no discrimination because of characteristics such as disability.

263.summary: Being criminally responsible from 14 means: young people aged 14 and over who break criminal laws are punished.
263.whyCorrect: Juvenile criminal law applies to them, which focuses mainly on education rather than punishment.
263.background: Children under 14 are not criminally responsible in Germany and cannot be punished (Section 19 of the Criminal Code). From 14, the Youth Courts Act applies to young people. A youth court can order, for example, community service, a social training course, victim–offender mediation, youth detention or, in serious cases, youth imprisonment. The aim is for young people to learn from their mistakes and not commit further crimes. Juvenile criminal law can also still be applied to 18- to 20-year-olds.
263.otherOptions: Young people are not treated like adults but under special juvenile criminal law. Parents do not share the punishment with their children – punishment is always personal. And “are not punished” only applies to children under 14.
263.memoryTip: Under 14: no punishment. From 14: juvenile criminal law.

264.summary: People wear colourful costumes and masks on Rose Monday (Rosenmontag).
264.whyCorrect: Rose Monday is the highlight of the carnival season, also called Fastnacht or Fasching.
264.background: Carnival is celebrated above all in the Rhineland, in Mainz and in southern Germany, and depending on the region it is also called Fastnacht or Fasching. The “fifth season” traditionally begins on 11 November at 11:11 am; it reaches its peak in the week before Ash Wednesday. On Rose Monday, large parades with floats move through cities such as Cologne, Düsseldorf and Mainz, people are in costume and sweets are thrown into the crowd. Ash Wednesday marks the start of the Christian season of Lent before Easter.
264.otherOptions: On 1 May, Labour Day, there are rallies and May festivals. At the Oktoberfest in Munich, many people wear traditional dress such as dirndls and lederhosen, but no masks. Pentecost is a Christian festival 50 days after Easter.

265.summary: Anyone who wants to marry must first go to the registry office (Standesamt).
265.whyCorrect: You give notice of marriage at the registry office; in Germany only a civil wedding is legally valid.
265.background: The couple gives notice of marriage at the registry office where they live and presents documents, such as IDs and birth certificates; foreign nationals often need additional papers, such as a certificate of no impediment to marriage. The wedding itself then takes place before a registrar. A church or other religious ceremony is also possible but has no legal effect. You can marry from the age of 18.
265.otherOptions: At the residents’ registration office you register your address, the public order office deals with public order, and the employment agency helps with job searches – none of them is responsible for weddings.

266.summary: Night-time quiet hours in Germany usually begin at 10 pm.
266.whyCorrect: From 10 pm to 6 am, you should avoid noise so as not to disturb the neighbours.
266.background: Quiet hours are regulated in the states’ noise and pollution control laws and usually also in the house rules. During this time you should, for example, not play loud music, not drill and keep parties quiet. Many house rules also set quiet times on Sundays and public holidays, sometimes also at midday. Anyone who disturbs the night-time quiet risks trouble with the neighbours and, if repeated, a fine.
266.otherOptions: Quiet hours do not depend on sunset or on when the neighbours go to bed. And they do not begin at midnight, but already at 10 pm.

267.summary: The parents must respect the decision of their adult daughter.
267.whyCorrect: At 22, the woman is an adult and may decide for herself whom she lives with.
267.background: Article 2 of the Basic Law protects every person’s right to the free development of their personality. This includes deciding for yourself whom you love, whom you live with and whom you marry. From the age of 18, parents no longer decide this. They may give their opinion and advice, but must not exert pressure. Anyone who forces someone into marriage through violence or threats commits a crime (forced marriage, Section 237 of the Criminal Code).
267.otherOptions: The parents may not bring their daughter back against her will – that could even be a crime such as coercion or false imprisonment. They cannot report her to the police, because she is doing nothing forbidden. And the parents may not choose a husband for their daughter.
